components.name: Filtering and search
components.summary: Narrow a list to the rows that matter with filter pills that apply as you tick, show counts, and live in the URL.
components.problem: Hiring teams work through hundreds of listings and candidates and need to narrow them quickly. If every screen filters differently, people relearn the controls each time and links to a filtered list break.
components.solution: Use the filter bar (pills) for list pages and the filter panel only for search across many fields. List values apply on tick with match counts, typed values apply on Enter, and the whole query is stored in the URL.

steps.t: Show one or two of the most used fields as dashed pills next to Filter (F). Everything else sits behind Filter in a type-ahead list grouped into most used and all fields.
Opening a pill shows its values with the number of rows each one matches. Ticking a list value applies it at once; numbers and dates apply on Enter.
An applied filter becomes a solid pill that reads as a sentence: field, operator, value, for example "Status is any of Live, Expiring". Its remove button sits on the left.
Clear and the result count sit straight after the pills, so the person sees what is applied and how many rows match without opening anything.
Every change to a filter updates the URL, so reload, back and a shared link all reproduce the same list.
If nothing matches, the table is replaced by a zero results state with Clear filters as the action.

whenToUse.t: On any list page with more than one screen of rows: listings, candidates, pipeline, inbox.
When people mostly narrow by two or three known fields such as status, location or team.
Use the filter panel instead of pills when there are many fields to filter by, as in candidate search, and the panel can stay open beside the results.

whenNotToUse.t: To find one known record by name or ID. Use search in the command palette (⌘K) or the view's search (/) instead.
For view settings that always have a value, such as a chart's date range or Daily vs Weekly. Pills are removable, so these use a rectangle (segmented control or dropdown) instead.
When several tables share one page. Filters in the URL become ambiguous, so filter each table locally and do not persist.

guidelines.t: Filters act on the whole collection, not just the rows loaded on screen. The count says so: "Showing 5 of 412 candidates".
Apply on tick because TwoUX's queries return fast; filter interactively when results come back almost instantly and in a batch when they are slow.
If a query will take more than about a second, dim the results and show a progress indicator rather than redrawing after every tick.
Show match counts on every list option so people avoid combinations that return nothing.
Never put a filter row inside each column header. The pill bar keeps the whole query in one visible, shareable place.
Validate filter values read from the URL and fall back to defaults when they are invalid. Never put personal data in the URL.
Offer a plain search box alone when people know the exact name, such as a candidate's surname. Add pills when they choose among known values, such as stage or location.
Show and/or wording only once two or more filters are applied; one filter reads as a plain sentence.
Returning to a list by Back, the breadcrumb or the sidebar restores the filters the person left with.
When a page has two filterable lists, only the main one writes its filters to the URL; the other keeps its filters on screen only.

content.t: Pill text follows field, operator, value in sentence case: "Posted is in the last 30 days".
Zero results heading: "No listings match these filters", then one sentence suggesting the likeliest fix, then a Clear filters button.
Counts use the noun of the list: "14 listings", not "14 results".

accessibility.t: Announce the new result count in a polite live region after each change, without moving focus.
Each pill's remove button is its own Tab stop, named after its filter: "Remove Status filter".
The value list is a combobox with a listbox: arrow keys move, Space ticks, Enter applies a typed value, Esc closes and returns focus to the pill.
F to open Filter is a single-key shortcut, so it can be turned off in the shortcut sheet.

dos.t: Do keep the active query visible as pills at all times.
Do show how many rows each value matches.
Do write filters to the URL on every change.

donts.t: Don't hide applied filters behind a single "3 filters" badge on desktop.
Don't add an Apply button to a fast list filter; it adds a step for nothing.
Don't use the empty state illustration and copy for a failed load. That is an error state.

components.name: Saved views
components.summary: Store a filtered, sorted, column-chosen list under a name so people and teams return to it in one click.
components.problem: People rebuild the same filters every morning, and teams share screenshots of lists instead of links. Without one way to save, each screen invents its own favourites.
components.solution: When filters are on, Save view stores filters, sort and columns together with a name. Views show live counts, mark unsaved changes, and reproduce from the URL.

steps.t: Save view appears only once at least one filter, sort or column change differs from the default.
Save view asks for a name (required) and an optional description, validating duplicate names inline.
The view appears as a tab or sidebar item with its live row count, for example "Live 14".
If the person changes a saved view, its name shows an unsaved mark and the menu offers Update view, Save as new and Revert.
The view's state also lives in the URL, so a copied link opens the same view for anyone with access.

whenToUse.t: For lists people check repeatedly with the same filters, such as "My live listings" or "Closing this week".
To give a team a shared starting point that everyone sees the same way.

whenNotToUse.t: For a one-off filter. The URL already makes it shareable; use Filtering and search.
For per-person display choices such as row density or wrapping. Those belong in the Columns menu and are remembered automatically.

guidelines.t: A view stores filters, sort order, visible columns and grouping. Opening it restores all four.
A default view loads when the page opens, unless the URL already carries filters.
Changing a saved view never overwrites it silently. Updating needs an explicit Update view.
Deleting a view uses a simple confirmation, because a team view can be in other people's sidebars.
Keep the number of pinned views short; long rows of tabs slow the choice down.
Group the views list into Team views and My views, and add a search box once there are more than about ten.
People can set any view as their own default with Set as default. It is unavailable while the current view has unsaved changes, and the reason is shown.
Update view shows the filters before and after in the menu, then saves with Undo in the toast.
People can drop unsaved changes in any of three ways: Revert, choosing the view again, or Clear filters.

content.t: Name views by what they contain, not who made them: "Closing this week", not "Rahul's view".
Menu actions: "Save view", "Save as new view", "Update view", "Revert changes", "Delete view".

accessibility.t: The unsaved mark is text ("Edited") as well as a dot, so it does not rely on colour.
Confirm a save with a status message announced politely, not a moved focus.

dos.t: Do show the live count on each view.
Do mark a modified view and offer Revert.

donts.t: Don't save a view automatically when filters change.
Don't store a view only in local storage; it must reproduce from its link.

components.name: Selection and bulk actions
components.summary: Pick rows with X or checkboxes, then act on all of them from one bar above the table that says how many rows it will touch.
components.problem: Extending, closing or exporting listings one by one is slow, and bulk actions placed in different spots on each page are missed or misfired.
components.solution: Selecting rows shows the bulk action bar directly above the table, with the actions, the count and Esc to clear. Filters and column headers stay where they were.

steps.t: Select a row with its checkbox or X; ⇧J extends the selection downward. The header checkbox selects only the rows on the current page.
The bulk action bar appears directly above the table: the actions with their shortcuts on the left, the count ("2 listings selected") and Clear selection (Esc) on the right.
If more rows match than are on screen, the bar offers "Select all 412", and the count updates to say so.
Choosing an action runs it on the selected rows. Reversible actions show a toast with Undo; irreversible ones confirm first.
If an action cannot apply to some selected rows, say how many and why before it runs.

whenToUse.t: When the same action is often applied to many rows: extend, close, assign, export, ask the assistant.

whenNotToUse.t: For an action on one record. Use the row's actions or the side panel.
When the action needs per-row input, such as different closing dates. Use inline editing in the data grid.

guidelines.t: Every bulk action is also available on a single selected row. The bar only adds the multi-row case.
Labels are verb plus noun and say how many rows: "Close 2 listings".
Keep the filters visible while rows are selected; the bar sits between the filters and the table instead of replacing the toolbar.
Changing filters or sort clears the selection, so an action never touches rows the person can no longer see.
Bulk results confirm in one toast ("2 listings extended") with Undo, not one toast per row.
A bulk action that can't apply to the current selection stays in the bar as unavailable, with a reason: "Available when all selected listings are Live".
The bar holds every action that can run on more than one record; row menus never offer "Close all" or similar.
Order bar actions the same way as the page header: status actions first, destructive near the end, the main action last.
Beyond four actions, the rest go in a More menu in the bar.

content.t: Count format: "2 listings selected" in the bar, "2 of 24 selected" in the table footer.
Destructive bulk confirmations name the count and the consequence: "Close 2 listings? They stop taking applications now."

accessibility.t: Selected rows set aria-selected="true"; the selection is also shown with a tick, not colour alone.
Announce the selection count when it changes.
The header checkbox shows an indeterminate state when some rows are selected.
Unavailable bulk actions use aria-disabled so their reason can be reached by keyboard.

dos.t: Do keep the count in the bar beside Clear selection, and name it in the toolbar's label so screen readers hear it before the actions.
Do offer Undo after a reversible bulk action.

donts.t: Don't replace the filter bar with the bulk bar; people lose sight of what they selected from.
Don't silently skip rows an action can't apply to.

components.name: Inline editing and validation
components.summary: Edit values where they are shown, check each field when the person leaves it, and summarise every problem on submit.
components.problem: Errors that appear while typing feel like nagging, and errors that only appear after submit are hard to find. Each form in a product tends to validate at a different moment.
components.solution: Validate a field when the person leaves it. In the data grid, Enter edits, Enter saves and Esc cancels, and invalid values stay in edit. On submit, a summary counts the problems and moves focus to the first.

steps.t: Show which values are editable: an edit affordance on hover in the side panel, cell focus in the data grid.
Enter starts editing; Enter saves and Esc cancels.
Check the value when the person leaves the field, never on the first keystroke.
If invalid, keep the cell or field in edit with a red outline, an icon and a message under it that says how to fix it.
Once the person is fixing an error, re-check on each keystroke so the message clears as soon as the value is valid.
On submit of a longer form, show a summary at the top that counts the problems and links to each, and move focus to the first field in error.

whenToUse.t: For values people change often, one at a time, such as a listing's closing date or owner.
Across many rows in the data grid, where the same property is edited on many records.

whenNotToUse.t: For creating a record or changing several dependent fields at once. Use a form in the side panel or a full page.
In the list table. Only the data grid supports cell editing.

guidelines.t: Read and edit states use the same type size and weight so text does not jump.
In a filtered or sorted table, keep an edited row in place until the person refreshes, so it does not vanish under their cursor.
Keep the submit button enabled on longer forms; pressing it runs validation and shows the summary.
Mark required fields. If most fields are required, mark the optional ones instead.
Server errors that belong to a field appear on that field; errors that belong to no field appear in a banner above the form actions.
The error summary is in addition to field messages, never instead of them.
Show requirements before anyone gets them wrong: constraint text under the field ("3 to 80 characters") and a format example. An error should never be the first time people see a rule.
Warnings are not errors: a field warning ("Salary is below the range for similar roles") is shown in amber text and does not block saving.
After submit, stay on the form until the server answers, with a spinner in the Save button. Never redirect first and lose the input.
If a slow submit must leave the page, the result message links back to the form with the values and errors restored.
A server error that belongs to a field, such as "A listing with this reference already exists", goes on that field, not in the banner.

content.t: Required message: "[Field] is required", for example "Closing date is required".
Say what is wrong and how to fix it in one sentence: "Salary must be a number, like 32000".
Summary heading: "2 problems to fix", each a link to its field.
Format errors start with Enter: "Enter a valid email address, like name@example.co.uk".
Length errors give the count: "Job title has too many characters. 92 of 80." Counters read "Character count: 12/80".
Don't use a generic top message such as "Fix the errors on this page"; the summary lists each problem.

accessibility.t: Errors are text, not just a red border; colour is a second cue.
Link each message to its field with aria-describedby and set aria-invalid on the field.
On submit, move focus to the first field in error.
In the grid, Enter or F2 enters edit, Esc restores grid navigation and may undo the edit.
Placeholders are examples only; labels and constraint text carry the instructions, because placeholder text disappears and often fails contrast.

dos.t: Do validate on blur and clear the error as soon as it is fixed.
Do keep save and cancel visible while editing.

donts.t: Don't show errors on fields the person hasn't reached yet.
Don't rely on a top summary alone.
Don't report a failed save in a toast; keep the field in error with Retry.

components.name: Empty, loading and error states
components.summary: One rule set for the three states every view has before or instead of data: loading, nothing to show, and failed.
components.problem: A blank table can mean loading, no data, no matches or a failure. When screens handle these differently, people wait for data that never comes or give up on data that was about to arrive.
components.solution: Skeleton rows while loading, an empty state with one next step when there is nothing, a zero results state when filters match nothing, and an error state that keeps the filters and offers Try again.

steps.t: Under about one second, show nothing extra. Beyond that, keep the table's shape with skeleton rows.
If the load succeeds with no records, replace the table with an empty state: what goes here, and one action to add it.
If records exist but filters match none, show the zero results state with Clear filters.
If the load fails, replace the table with an error state that says what failed, keeps the filters and offers Try again (R).
When a refresh fails after data has loaded, keep the old data on screen and show a warning beside the refresh time.

whenToUse.t: On every table, grid, chart card, panel and assistant answer that loads data.

whenNotToUse.t: For a brand new workspace with nothing set up. Use Onboarding to an empty workspace with the setup checklist.

guidelines.t: Never show "No listings" before loading has finished; people stop waiting and miss the data.
Skeletons for structured content (tables, cards); a spinner for a single element such as a button or expanding row; a progress bar beyond about ten seconds.
Empty and zero results states replace the table and its headers, so screen readers don't meet an empty table.
Every state offers a next step. No dead ends.
Errors never use the empty state component; they use the error state or a banner.
Show when data was last updated after each refresh.

Charts follow the same states with chart-specific shapes: the plot skeleton while loading, an empty state for no data, a no match state with Clear filters after filtering, and an error state with Try again, each inside the chart card so the title and controls stay.

Manual refresh lives in the table header as an icon button labelled "Refresh listings", next to "Last updated 2 minutes ago". Add a refresh button only where data changes while people watch; other views refresh on load.
During a refresh keep the current rows on screen and usable; only the refresh button shows a spinner.
If a refresh takes longer than about ten seconds, show a "Taking longer than usual" status beside the refresh time; if it partly fails, show a warning status there with what failed and Try again.
Wrap each region (table, chart card, side panel) in its own error boundary, so a crash shows an error state in that region and the rest of the page still works.
Inside a table or read-only details, an empty value shows a muted hyphen (-) with the accessible name "Not set". Never use a dash for a real zero; show 0.
Keep the count in the table heading even when empty: "Listings (0)".

content.t: Empty: "No listings yet" plus "Create listing". Zero results: "No listings match these filters" plus "Clear filters".
Error: "Couldn't load listings", then the likeliest cause, then "Your filters are kept." Avoid "sorry" and error codes.
Loading text names the thing without articles or end punctuation: "Loading listings".
The empty state's action uses the same label as the header button it mirrors ("Create listing") and is a secondary button, since the header already has the primary.
An empty state description explains why it is empty and never repeats the heading or button text.

accessibility.t: Announce loading, loaded counts and failures as status messages without moving focus.
Hide decorative empty state illustrations from screen readers with empty alt text.
Error states are identified in text, not only with a red icon.
The refresh button has loading text ("Refreshing listings"), and the new "Last updated" time is announced politely.

dos.t: Do keep the layout stable from skeleton to data.
Do keep filters when a load fails.

donts.t: Don't use a full-page spinner for a table load.
Don't show a frame-only skeleton with no placeholder rows.
Don't write jokes into error messages.

components.name: Undo and destructive actions
components.summary: Decide between Undo after the fact and a confirmation before it, using one test: can the action be reversed, and who else does it reach?
components.problem: Confirming everything trains people to click Yes without reading; confirming nothing loses data. Teams pick differently on every screen.
components.solution: Reversible actions run at once and offer Undo in a toast and with ⌘Z. Irreversible actions, or ones that reach people outside the workspace, confirm in a dialog that states the consequence, with the safe option focused.

steps.t: Ask: can TwoUX reverse this fully? Extending, renaming, archiving and moving can be reversed; deleting, emailing candidates and closing a listing that has notified applicants cannot.
Reversible: run it, then show a toast such as "2 listings extended" with Undo. ⌘Z undoes the last action too.
Irreversible: open a confirmation dialog titled with the action and count, stating what happens and what is kept.
Buttons name the outcome: the safe option ("Keep open") and the action ("Close listings"). Focus starts on the safe option.
For severe actions that also remove related records, such as deleting a workspace, ask the person to type the name.

whenToUse.t: Undo: for every reversible change made by a person or applied by the assistant.
Dialog: for deletion, sending to people outside the workspace, and actions that cascade.

whenNotToUse.t: Don't confirm routine reversible actions; offer Undo instead.
Don't use a toast as the only record of something important; important outcomes also appear in the record's activity.

guidelines.t: Scale friction to severity: none for low-risk, one dialog for high-risk, typed confirmation only for the rarest, most damaging actions.
The dialog body names the items, the consequence and what stays: "The 140 people who already applied stay in your pipeline."
Undo stays reachable after the toast goes: ⌘Z and the record's activity both reverse the last action.
An Undo toast stays while hovered or focused and does not close while the person is reading it.
The action button uses the danger style and sits to the right of the safe option, never on its own.

content.t: Dialog title is a question with the count: "Close 2 listings?"
Never "Are you sure?", "Yes" or "OK". Use outcome labels.
Toast: past tense plus Undo: "Listing archived. Undo".

accessibility.t: Confirmation dialogs use role alertdialog with aria-labelledby and aria-describedby.
Focus moves to the least destructive button, Tab is trapped, Esc cancels and focus returns to the trigger.
Toasts are announced as status messages; Undo also has a keyboard path (⌘Z) because toast actions are hard to reach with a keyboard.

dos.t: Do offer Undo after every reversible change, including bulk and assistant changes.
Do state the consequence in the dialog body.

donts.t: Don't focus the destructive button by default.

components.name: Notifications: inbox, bell, toast or email digest
components.summary: Route every message by one question: does it need this person to act? Things that need you go to the Inbox; your own results go in a toast; nothing gets a separate bell list.
components.problem: Products grow a bell, an inbox, toasts, banners and emails that overlap, so people get the same news three times and miss the one that needed them.
components.solution: The Inbox is the one place for things that need you (agent approvals and questions, listings about to close, mentions, assignments). Toasts only confirm your own actions. Workspace-wide problems use a banner. Email sends a digest of open Inbox items to people who are away.

steps.t: Did this person just do it? Confirm with a toast, or with nothing if the change is already visible.
Does it need this person to act or reply? Put it in the Inbox. It stays until marked done (E) or snoozed (⇧H).
Does it affect everyone's use of the workspace, such as a broken connection? Show a banner on the affected pages until fixed.
Is the person away from TwoUX and is something waiting on them? Send an email digest of open Inbox items, at the frequency they chose.
Needs nothing from anyone? Record it in the record's activity only.

whenToUse.t: Whenever a feature wants to tell someone something. Pick the channel with the steps above before designing the message.

whenNotToUse.t: For validation of what someone typed. Use field messages from Inline editing and validation.
For errors that need a retry. A toast disappears and cannot hold Retry reliably; use a banner or the error state.

guidelines.t: No separate bell list. The Inbox count is the only unread count; when the sidebar is hidden, a small inbox button with the same count replaces it.
Toasts never carry critical warnings or errors and never auto-dismiss something the person must act on.
Don't resend notifications people have not acted on; let them set email frequency and channels.
Trivial updates go nowhere but activity. Notification fatigue makes people ignore the important ones.

content.t: Toasts are past tense and short: "Listing published". Three lines at most.
Banners say what is affected and what to do: "Workable is disconnected. Reconnect to keep importing candidates."

accessibility.t: Toasts and count changes are announced as status messages.
Toasts must not cover the focused element; they appear in an empty corner.
Anything shown only in a vanishing toast must also be findable elsewhere, such as activity or the Inbox.

dos.t: Do send everything that needs action to the Inbox.
Do give people control over email frequency.

donts.t: Don't add a bell next to the Inbox.
Don't use a toast for errors that need a follow-up.

components.name: Record detail: side panel, overlay or full page
components.summary: Open a record in a side panel that pushes the list by default, overlay it on narrow or wide-content pages, and go to the full page for deep work.
components.problem: Opening records in modals hides the list people compare against; opening a full page every time loses their place. Teams pick a different container on every screen.
components.solution: Enter or a click opens the side panel in push mode. J and K move to the next record and the panel follows. Esc closes. Open (⇧↵) goes to the full page. Overlay replaces push below about 1100px or when the content needs width.

steps.t: Enter or a click on a row opens the side panel. The row stays highlighted and the list stays usable.
The panel has a control bar (previous, next, position, open full page, close), then ID, title and status, then tabs and sections.
J and K move to the next or previous row; the panel follows without closing.
Open (⇧↵) moves to the full record page, with breadcrumbs back to the list and the same filters.
Esc closes the panel and returns focus to the row that opened it.

whenToUse.t: Push side panel: on list pages people work through one record after another (listings, candidates, inbox).
Overlay side panel: when the page is narrower than about 1100px, or holds wide tables or dashboards that pushing would crush.
Full page: for long records, history, or editing many related sections.

whenNotToUse.t: Don't use a modal dialog for record detail; it hides the rows people compare against. Modals are for confirmations.
Don't open the detail inline as an expanding row; expanded rows pile up and clutter the table.

guidelines.t: A split view never replaces the full page; the panel is for deciding the next step, the page is for everything about one record.
Only one secondary panel of a kind at a time; the assistant and record detail share the same side panel slot.
Keep the identifying columns visible next to a pushed panel so people know which row they are on.
People can switch push and overlay with ⇧P, and the choice is remembered.
With several rows selected, the panel shows a useful summary of the selection, not a list of names.
The side panel shares the single right-hand slot with the assistant and help panels; opening one replaces the other, and closing it restores the previous one.
If a form in the panel has unsaved changes, J, K, Esc and close ask before discarding (see Unsaved changes). Single-field edits save on Enter and never ask.
Section actions sit in each section's header on the right ("Edit details"); record-wide actions sit in the panel footer.
The Details section shows absolute timestamps with their source: "Created 6 November 2026, 09:14 GMT by Priya Shah".

content.t: Empty fields say "Add", so the gap is also the way to fill it.
Timestamps are relative with the exact date on hover.
Fields the person can't edit are shown as read-only text with the reason on hover, such as "Set by the job board feed".

accessibility.t: A push panel is non-modal: it sits in the focus order after the list and never traps focus.
An overlay panel that covers content behaves as a modal dialog: focus moves in, Tab is trapped, Esc closes and focus returns.
The panel must not fully hide the focused row.

dos.t: Do keep J/K working while the panel is open.
Do return focus to the row on close.

donts.t: Don't open record detail in a centred modal.
Don't open a second panel on top of the first.

components.name: Keyboard-first navigation
components.summary: Every action has a key shown on its button. J/K move, Enter opens, Esc steps back one layer at a time, ⌘K runs anything, ⌘J asks the assistant.
components.problem: Power users triage hundreds of rows a day. If shortcuts differ per screen, or Esc sometimes closes a panel and sometimes clears a selection, people stop trusting the keyboard.
components.solution: One keyboard model across TwoUX: the same keys mean the same thing everywhere, shortcuts are shown on buttons, ? opens the full list, and single-key shortcuts can be turned off.

steps.t: J and K move the row focus; X selects; ⇧J extends the selection.
Enter opens the focused row in the side panel; ⇧↵ opens the full page.
Esc closes the top-most layer only, in this order: open menu or popover, then text field edit, then dialog, then side panel, then selection.
⌘K opens the command palette: actions on the current selection first, then Go to. ↑↓ move, ↵ runs, Tab changes scope.
⌘J opens the assistant with the current selection and filters as context.
? opens the shortcut sheet, which also holds the switch for single-key shortcuts.

whenToUse.t: On every screen. A new action is not finished until it has a key, a place in ⌘K and a hint on its button.

whenNotToUse.t: Don't add single-key shortcuts inside text fields or the composer; there the keys type text.
Don't make a shortcut the only path to an action; every action is also a visible control.

guidelines.t: Show the shortcut on the button or menu item itself so people learn it by using the product.
Keep the set small and mnemonic: C create, E edit, F filter, T extend, D duplicate.
Avoid ⌘ plus a single key that the browser or OS owns, except deliberate, well-used ones such as ⌘K.
Single-key shortcuts can be turned off; ⌘ shortcuts stay on.
Focus is always visible and never lost to the page body when a row or panel disappears.
Use the same keys as tools people already know (J/K, ⌘K) instead of inventing new ones.

content.t: Hints use symbols: ⌘K, ⇧↵, Esc. Shown in a muted key cap after the label.
The shortcut sheet groups keys by Navigate, Table and Act.

accessibility.t: Everything works by keyboard alone.
Lists use roving tabindex so Tab enters and leaves a list in one step and arrows move inside it.
Single-character shortcuts can be turned off for screen reader and voice control users.
Closing a layer returns focus to the element that opened it.

dos.t: Do keep Esc's order the same on every screen.
Do list every shortcut in ? and in ⌘K.

donts.t: Don't let one Esc press close two layers.
Don't reuse a key for different actions on different pages.

components.name: Data export
components.summary: One Export menu on every table: choose what to include first, then the format, then copy instead of download if you want.
components.problem: People export to share with hiring managers or to work in a spreadsheet. When each table exports differently, they get files with hidden columns, raw field names or AI guesses mixed with real data.
components.solution: Export (⇧E) opens one menu: options first (visible columns only, include AI columns, selected rows or all matching rows), then formats, then copy to clipboard. The file matches what is on screen.

steps.t: Export sits in the table toolbar with the other global table actions, and in the bulk bar when rows are selected.
Options come first: rows (selected, or all N matching the filters), visible columns only, include AI columns.
Then the format (CSV, Excel), then Copy to clipboard for quick pastes.
Small exports download at once with a toast. Exports likely to take more than about ten seconds run in the background with progress, and finish with an Inbox item linking to the file.
If the export fails, say why and offer Try again in a banner, not a toast.

whenToUse.t: On any list table, data grid, breakdown table or chart that has a table view.

whenNotToUse.t: To share a view with a colleague inside TwoUX. Share the view's link instead (Saved views).
As a fix for missing analysis. If many people export the same table, add the analysis to the product.

guidelines.t: The file matches the screen: same rows, same visible columns, same order, column names as shown, not database field names.
AI columns are excluded by default and, when included, are named with a suffix such as "(AI)" so generated values are never mistaken for real data.
Say the scope in numbers before export: "Export 412 candidates".
Long exports do not block the page; people can keep working.

content.t: Menu label: "Export". Actions name the scope: "Export 2 rows as CSV".

accessibility.t: Announce "Export ready" or "Export failed" as a status message.
The export menu is a standard menu button reachable by keyboard; ⇧E opens it.

dos.t: Do export what the person sees.
Do label AI columns in the file.

donts.t: Don't put Export in a different place on each table.
Don't block the screen while a large export runs.

components.name: Comparison over time
components.summary: Every headline number says what it compares against: this period vs the previous period of the same length, with arrow, sign and colour.
components.problem: "312 applications" means nothing on its own. Teams add comparisons in different ways (vs last month, vs last year, percentage or absolute), so numbers on different screens can't be read together.
components.solution: TwoUX compares the current period with the previous period of the same length by default. Stats show the number, then the change with arrow, sign and colour, then what it is compared with. Charts draw the previous period as a dashed grey line behind the current one.

steps.t: Pick the period with one control above the chart: 7d, 30d, 90d. It drives every chart and stat on the page.
The stat leads with the number, then the change ("↑ 18%"), then the comparison in words ("vs 264 the 30 days before").
The line chart shows the previous period as a dashed grey line behind the current period, with a legend naming both.
Under the chart, the breakdown table shows current and previous side by side and the change in both units.
Every chart can switch to a table, which is also its accessible version.

whenToUse.t: For any KPI or trend on a dashboard, report or record header.
Next to a single figure in a record, compare with the board median instead of time, so people can judge it without opening a report.

whenNotToUse.t: When there is no previous period (new listing, new team). Show a dash, not "+100%".
To compare categories in one period. Use a bar chart or breakdown, not a time comparison.

guidelines.t: Never rely on colour alone for up or down; always add an arrow and a sign.
Green and red follow meaning, not direction. A fall in time to first apply is good.
Bars start at zero. Line charts may start elsewhere, but say so on the axis.
One y-axis per chart. Two measures with different scales get two charts side by side.
Keep each series the same colour on every chart; status colours never colour a series.
The current, incomplete period is marked as incomplete so a half week does not look like a drop.

content.t: Change text: "↑ 18% vs 264 the 30 days before". Units are always stated.
Chart footer names the source and when it updated: "updated 12 min ago".

accessibility.t: The change is read as text ("up 18 percent"), not only drawn as an arrow.
Chart points are reachable with the arrow keys, and the table view carries every number.

dos.t: Do say what every number is compared against.
Do use the previous period of the same length.

donts.t: Don't use two y-axes.
Don't show a percentage change from zero.

components.name: Onboarding to an empty workspace
components.summary: A new workspace shows a short setup checklist in the sidebar and empty states that each offer one way in: create, import or start from a template.
components.problem: A new team lands on empty tables and a blank assistant. Product tours get skipped and forgotten, and each feature invents its own first-run screen.
components.solution: "Get set up 3 / 5" sits in the sidebar until done or dismissed. Each empty page explains what goes there and offers the fastest way in. Templates open as drafts, never run on their own.

steps.t: Show a setup checklist in the sidebar with a count ("Get set up 3 / 5") and the next step underneath.
Each step is an action people need anyway: connect your careers page, invite the team, create a first listing, set team instructions, try a saved task.
Steps complete themselves when the thing is done anywhere in the product.
Each empty page explains what will appear and offers one primary way in, with import or a template as the second.
Templates open as an editable draft that names the tools it uses. Nothing runs until the person chooses Run.
The checklist can be dismissed and reopened from Settings.

whenToUse.t: For a new workspace, and for a feature someone opens for the first time (a blank slate).

whenNotToUse.t: Don't open a product tour or deck of cards on first login; show help when people reach the feature.
For a list that is empty because of filters. Use the zero results state.

guidelines.t: Keep the checklist to five steps or fewer, ordered by value to the team.
Offer starter content (sample listings) only if it is clearly marked and easy to remove; keep a plain empty state for when it is gone.
Show help in context and on request, not up front.
The assistant's empty state offers two or three tasks based on what is on screen, not a blank "How can I help?".
Say early what the assistant can and can't do with the workspace's data.
Track checklist steps as tasks done or not done, not progress inside a task. A step left halfway still shows as not done.
Recommend a setting when it helps, but never stop people choosing another one. Warn only when their choice blocks the goal of the step.
Show steps that can't start yet and say what they need first, such as "Connect your careers page first". Don't hide them.
Support both people who read first and people who try first: a short line and Learn more on each step, and an action that starts the task straight away.
Once the checklist is dismissed it stays dismissed on every page until reopened from Settings.

content.t: Blank slate titles invite the action: "Create your first listing". Body says why in one sentence.
Checklist steps start with a verb and say the benefit: "Connect your careers page to import roles automatically".

accessibility.t: The checklist progress is text ("3 of 5 done"), not only a ring.
Completing a step is announced as a status message.
Recommendation popovers attached to a step open one at a time, never on their own, and close with Esc.

dos.t: Do show progress through setup.
Do give every empty page a way in.

donts.t: Don't block the product behind a setup wizard.
Don't run a template without the person choosing Run.

components.name: Ask about what's on screen
components.summary: ⌘J or Ask opens the assistant beside the data with the current selection and filters as removable context chips, so the scope of every answer is visible.
components.problem: People ask "why are these doing badly?" about the rows in front of them. A floating chat with no context makes them retype what they can see, and answers silently cover the wrong set of records.
components.solution: The assistant opens in the same side panel as record detail. Selection and active filters become context chips automatically; removing a chip narrows the scope. Starters are based on what is on screen. Answers lead with the figure, then a table, then the reason.

steps.t: Open with ⌘J anywhere, or Ask in the bulk bar. No floating chat bubble on every page.
The composer shows context chips for what the assistant can see: "2 listings", "Status is Live, Expiring". Remove a chip to narrow it; @ adds a record.
The empty state offers two or three tasks based on the context, as chips, then the composer.
The answer leads with the figure, then a table, then the reason, with record IDs as citations.
Follow-ups appear under the answer as muted rows; any table in the answer can open as a filtered view.

whenToUse.t: For questions about records the person can see or has selected: compare, explain, summarise.
When the answer will be checked against the list beside it.

whenNotToUse.t: To change records. The assistant proposes; see Propose then apply.
For filtering a list by known fields. Filter pills are faster than typing.

guidelines.t: Scope is always visible and editable; the assistant never reads more than the chips say unless the person widens it.
If the answer needs records outside the chips, ask before widening (see Clarifying before acting).
A caveat sits by the composer and is specific: "Uses your workspace data only. Check figures before you act on them."
Every message aligns to the same side in the side panel and on the page; who wrote it is shown by name ("You", "Assistant"), not by alignment.
The composer is pinned to the bottom and only the thread scrolls. While someone reads or copies older messages, new output doesn't scroll them away; show "New answer ↓" instead.
The Ask entry point is a secondary button. It never becomes a second primary button on the page and carries no AI styling.
After context is added, the assistant says what it will use in one line: "Using 2 listings and team file Salary bands 2026." People can correct it before anything runs.
Connecting an outside tool happens in the thread as a short step card, one step at a time, collapsing to "Connected as Leeds hiring team". People don't leave for settings.
Errors keep the question: say what failed (no access, connection lost, service error), that nothing changed, and offer Try again with the question still in the composer.
A refusal says plainly what the assistant won't do and what it can do instead: "I can't rank candidates for rejection. I can summarise each application against the role's criteria."

content.t: Call it Assistant. Say what it did ("Read 2 listings and 3,000 views"), not that it is AI. No "magic" or "smart".
Starters are broad, runnable tasks, not niche examples.

accessibility.t: Streamed answers are announced once complete, not word by word.
⌘J returns focus to where it was when the panel closes.
The thread is a region named "Assistant conversation"; each finished answer is announced once through a hidden live region.

dos.t: Do turn selection and filters into chips automatically.
Do lead answers with the number.

donts.t: Don't add a floating chat bubble to every page.
Don't open with a blank "How can I help?".

components.name: Propose, then apply
components.summary: The assistant never edits on its own: it lists suggested changes with checkboxes, the person applies them in one step, each change shows its progress, and Undo reverses all of it.
components.problem: When AI edits records directly, people can't see what changed or trust it with real data. When every feature invents its own approval flow, nobody knows whether clicking a suggestion has already changed something.
components.solution: Changes arrive as a Suggested changes card: one row per change with what changes, an Edit and a Dismiss. Apply N changes (⌘↵) turns the card into a step card that ticks off each change as the table updates. A toast offers Undo.

steps.t: The answer ends with "Suggested changes · 2", each a row with a checkbox, the change and its effect ("New closing date 6 Dec").
"Nothing changes until you apply" sits next to the buttons: Dismiss, Edit, Apply 2 changes ⌘↵.
The person unticks, edits or dismisses individual changes without regenerating the whole proposal.
Apply turns the card into a step card: each change gets a spinner then a tick, with a counter "1 / 2". The table updates row by row.
When done, a toast confirms ("2 changes applied") with Undo; ⌘Z also works.
If a change fails, its step says why and offers Retry; the others stay applied.

whenToUse.t: Whenever the assistant or an agent would change records: rename, extend, close, reassign.

whenNotToUse.t: For answers that change nothing; just answer.
For actions the person set to Allow in agent permissions; those run and are logged, with Undo where possible.
For changes that reach people outside the workspace, such as emailing candidates. Those also need explicit approval of the message itself (see Agents acting on your behalf).

guidelines.t: A proposal shows the consequence of each change before it runs, including whether it can be undone.
Approve is never pre-selected or auto-focused for risky changes.
If applying needs to deviate from the proposal, stop and explain rather than change something else.
The proposal is the same component everywhere: assistant answers, agent runs and the Inbox.

content.t: Each change is a verb and object with its effect: "Extend Operations Coordinator by 30 days. New closing date 6 Dec."
Apply button says the count: "Apply 2 changes".

accessibility.t: Step progress and completion are announced as status messages.
Apply has a keyboard shortcut (⌘↵) and focus does not jump to it automatically.

dos.t: Do let people untick individual changes.
Do offer Undo after applying.

donts.t: Don't apply anything from inside the answer text.
Don't regenerate the whole proposal to fix one change.

components.name: Showing reasoning and progress
components.summary: While working, say the current step in words with a running timer and a Stop; when done, collapse to "Thought for 2.1s · 4 steps" that opens on request.
components.problem: A bare spinner for ten seconds makes people think the assistant is stuck, and a wall of reasoning buries the answer. Without one rule, each surface shows progress differently.
components.solution: Thinking shows "Thinking" with a timer, then step titles with one line of detail. Send becomes Stop. When the answer starts, the steps collapse into one summary line that stays in the history.

steps.t: Under about one second, show nothing; stream the answer straight away.
Otherwise show "Thinking" with a running timer and the send button becomes Stop.
Each step appears with a short title and one line of detail: "Reading 9 listings".
Beyond about ten seconds, show the current step with an estimate, or a progress bar when the total is known ("3 of 50 rows").
When the answer starts, collapse to "Thought for 2.1s · 4 steps", expandable on click.
Stop keeps what was done so far, marks the run as stopped, and offers Regenerate.

whenToUse.t: Any assistant answer, agent run or AI column run that takes more than a second.

whenNotToUse.t: To justify an answer. Step text is a progress report, not proof; use citations for evidence.

guidelines.t: Show what was read and done, with counts and time, in neutral words. No first-person "I'm thinking hard".
Keep proposed, done and evidence apart: plan steps, completed steps, and citations are three different things.
Step states have one look everywhere: queued, running, waiting for you, done, skipped, failed, stopped.
Stop is always visible while anything runs and acts at once.
Never show credentials, token counts or raw system prompts in steps.
Collapsed by default in the side panel, where the answer is the main content.

Two stages: working (nothing to show yet: step text and timer) and writing (the answer streams). Keep a small working indicator until the last part has arrived, so a pause in streaming doesn't look like the end.
Stream only prose. Tables, lists of records and files render in place as a skeleton with "Loading 12 listings" until complete, then appear whole.
Thinking is reasoning; steps that read or change data are execution. Execution goes in the agent run or step card, never inside "Thinking".
Offer "Answer now" only when a useful answer exists from the work so far; what was done stays visible.
Show thinking expanded by default only where the answer isn't the main content, such as a generated column cell's detail.

Summaries count honestly: "2 of 5 steps" for steps in order, "3 done · 1 running · 1 queued" for parallel steps; add failed and stopped only when non-zero, and end with why it stopped: "2 of 5 steps · stopped".
A group's status is its most urgent child's: failed over waiting over running over done. Nest steps two levels at most.

content.t: Step titles are present participles while running ("Reading 9 listings") and past tense when done ("Read 9 listings").
Duration uses rounded values: "Thought for 7s".

accessibility.t: Announce the current step politely and the finished state once; don't announce every token.
Step state uses icon shape as well as colour.
The working label stays the same text ("Thinking") while it runs, so screen readers aren't re-reading a changing label.

dos.t: Do name the current step in words.
Do keep the collapsed summary in the conversation history.

donts.t: Don't show a bare looping animation for long waits.
Don't swap the label for streaming reasoning text; it flickers.

components.name: Clarifying before acting
components.summary: When the answer would change the result, ask with a question card above the composer: options with a recommended default, number keys, Skip and Next.
components.problem: An assistant that guesses rewrites the wrong listings; one that asks too much becomes a form. Without a rule, each feature decides differently when to ask.
components.solution: Ask only when the answer changes the result, at most three questions, one at a time. Each has a recommended option first, a one-line explanation per option, and "Use defaults" to skip the rest.

steps.t: Before acting, check whether the request is ambiguous in a way that changes the outcome (which listings, which period, who receives it).
If yes, show the question card docked above the composer: "1 / 2", the question, then options.
Options have a title and one line each, the recommended one first and marked, Other last with free text.
Number keys 1 to 4 pick an option; Previous, Skip and Next ↵ move through the questions.
The thread shows "Waiting for your answer" with a timer; in an agent run the step is marked Needs you and appears in the Inbox.
Once answered, the card collapses into a one-line summary of the choice, and the work continues.

whenToUse.t: When the request is ambiguous and the action is costly to get wrong.
When an agent hits a decision it is not allowed to make alone.

whenNotToUse.t: When the answer can be inferred from context chips or retrieved from data; don't ask what you already know.
For low-stakes answers; answer first and offer follow-ups instead.
For approving a concrete change; use Propose then apply.

guidelines.t: At most three questions per request, one at a time.
Every question has a default and "Use defaults" skips the rest.
Options before free text; the composer stays available for anything the options miss.
Say why the answer matters in the option's line ("Leaves listings that are doing well alone").
An unanswered question never blocks forever; in a scheduled run it expires and the run reports that nothing ran.
Ask first when the stakes are high or confidence is low; otherwise answer for the common case and offer follow-up options to narrow it.
If the person may not know the answer, say where to find it: "Salary bands are in Team files" with a link.
Values needed to carry out an action (dates, amounts) are not clarifying questions; use an input card (see Asking for details inside the answer).

content.t: Questions are short and specific: "Which titles should I rewrite?"
Mark the default "(Recommended)" in text, not only with a colour.

accessibility.t: Options are a radio group: arrows move, Space or the number key selects, Enter goes to Next.
Focus moves into the card when it appears and returns to the composer when it closes.

dos.t: Do put the recommended option first.
Do let people skip with defaults.

donts.t: Don't ask more than three questions.
Don't ask for information already in context.

components.name: Citing sources
components.summary: Every claim in an answer links to the record it came from by ID; clicking opens the record in the side panel, and the full page lists every record used.
components.problem: People can't act on an answer they can't check, and generic "Sources" lists at the bottom don't say which claim came from where.
components.solution: Citations are record IDs (LST-1044) placed right after the claim. They open the record in the side panel. The full-page view adds a Sources panel listing every record and file the answer used, and highlights the one being cited.

steps.t: Place the record ID straight after the sentence it supports.
Hover or focus shows a preview: record title, the figure used, when it was updated.
Click opens the record in the side panel next to the answer.
When the answer relied on a team file, cite the file by name.
Expanded to a full page, a Sources panel lists every record and file used, and citations highlight their source.

whenToUse.t: For every factual claim about workspace data in an answer, a generated cell or an agent step.

whenNotToUse.t: To decorate an answer with sources that don't support a specific claim; that builds false trust.
For reasoning steps; those are progress, not evidence (see Showing reasoning and progress).

guidelines.t: Cite at the claim, not in a list at the end, so people can tell sourced claims from synthesis.
Use descriptive citations (the record ID and title on hover), never "Source 1".
If a source is missing or deleted, say so openly instead of hiding the gap.
Keep citation style identical in answers, AI columns and agent runs.
Say what data the answer could not see, so people know when to rely on their own judgement.

content.t: Citations use the record ID as it appears in the product: "LST-1044".
Sources panel heading: "Sources", each item with title, type and last updated.

accessibility.t: Citations are links with accessible names that include the record title, not just the ID.
Citation previews open on focus as well as hover and close with Esc.

dos.t: Do link each claim to its record.
Do cite team files by name.

donts.t: Don't list sources only at the bottom.
Don't show a citation that doesn't support the claim.

components.name: Labelling AI output
components.summary: Mark generated content with one small origin mark next to it. No AI colour, no sparkle on every button, no "AI-powered" copy.
components.problem: People need to know which values a model wrote before they rely on them. But products that colour and sparkle every AI feature teach people to ignore the marks, and each team styles them differently.
components.solution: Generated content carries the origin mark and a line such as "Assistant · from your workspace data". Generated cells get the mark and a faint neutral tint and show when they were written. Buttons that start AI work look like every other button.

steps.t: Put the origin mark next to the generated output itself: under an answer, in a generated column header, on a drafted field.
When a whole group is generated, label the group header once instead of every item.
Say what produced it and from what: "Assistant · from your workspace data".
When a person edits a generated value, it becomes theirs and the mark goes; the original stays in history.
Exports name generated columns so they are never mistaken for real data.

whenToUse.t: For any value, text or chart the assistant or an agent produced that a person has not yet edited.

whenNotToUse.t: On buttons and entry points. Name the action instead ("Ask", "Suggest titles").
For non-generative automation such as rules or sorting.

guidelines.t: One mark, used only for generated output, never as decoration.
No separate AI colour. The tint on generated cells is a neutral surface so status and data colours keep their meaning.
Label the action, not the technology: "Summarised from 12 notes" beats "AI-generated".
Pair the mark with a way to see why: hovering it shows the sources and when it was written.
Feedback (good, bad) sits under every answer next to the mark.
The origin label is only for generative output. Rule-based automation (auto-close on expiry, duplicate detection) says what rule did it instead: "Closed automatically on 6 Dec".
The more control an action hands over, the clearer its label before it runs: "Runs as Listings checker · changes need approval" on a scheduled task.
If the whole surface is the assistant, don't repeat the mark on every part. The answer row carries it once.

content.t: Use "Assistant" as the name. Avoid "magic", "smart" and "AI-powered".
Mark text is short: "Assistant · 2 min ago".

accessibility.t: The mark has a text label for screen readers ("Written by Assistant"); it is not only an icon or a tint.
The tint meets contrast for the text on it.

dos.t: Do label generated output close to where it appears.
Do remove the mark once a person has edited the value.

donts.t: Don't give AI features their own colour or gradient.
Don't add a sparkle to every button that calls a model.

components.name: Agents acting on your behalf
components.summary: Agents work within permissions set per action (Off, Ask first, Allow), show every run as a list of steps, stop to wait for you through the Inbox, and can always be stopped.
components.problem: An agent that renames listings or emails candidates on a schedule acts while nobody watches. Without clear permissions, run history and a single place to approve, people either don't trust agents or are surprised by them.
components.solution: Permissions are set up front per action in plain words, with safe defaults. Each run is a timeline of steps with state. A step that needs approval waits, is marked Needs you and appears in the Inbox. Stop is always visible.

steps.t: Set permissions per action before the first run: Read defaults to Allow, changes to Ask first, anything that reaches people outside the workspace to Off.
The run shows each step with its state in shape and colour: done, running, waiting for you, skipped, failed.
Steps that pick rows show the filter they used and open it as a view.
A step that needs approval holds its action, is highlighted, says which permission caused it ("Edit listings is set to Ask first") and appears in the Inbox as Needs you.
Approve in the Inbox detail without leaving; the run continues. Rejecting is acknowledged in the run ("Skipped").
Stop is always visible. A stopped run keeps what it did and says what it didn't.

whenToUse.t: For multi-step work that runs without the person watching: scheduled tasks, long enrichment, follow-ups.

whenNotToUse.t: For high-risk actions where silence would count as consent. Those stay Off or Ask first, never notice-only.

guidelines.t: Permissions are explicit, editable and never buried in setup; changing one is one click from the run that hit it.
Each permission says in plain words what it allows: "Sends from your address".
Before a scheduled run makes changes, a notice lets people review or cancel.
Every run records who started it, when, what it read and changed, in an activity log that can be queried.
A request waiting for approval never blocks forever; it expires and reports that nothing ran.
Start with low automation; people raise it per action once they trust the results.
Agents are never disabled or deleted without someone choosing to.
When a run needs approval in a conversation, show an approval card above the composer with what will run, in plain words, and the tool name in code style.

For a tool the run will call again, offer "Allow once" and "Allow in this conversation". "Always allow" changes the agent's permission to Allow and is offered only for Read and reversible changes inside the workspace.
Before approval, say whether it can be undone and who else will see it: "Can be undone for 7 days. Applicants won't be notified."
After a decision the card closes at once and the thread keeps a resolved line: Approved, Rejected, Approved automatically, or Expired with "Nothing was sent."
If the person rejects, the assistant acknowledges it and carries on without that step: "Skipped emailing the Leeds team."
Irreversible actions use the confirmation dialog; when one record is affected the person types its name, when several the dialog lists them. Never both.

content.t: Run titles say the goal: "Rename low-performing listings". Footer: "Started by Rahul S. · 2 min ago · Every Monday".
Decisions are logged in past tense: "Approved", "Skipped: email hiring managers. Email is Off in permissions."

accessibility.t: Step states use icon shape and a word, not colour alone.
The approval card is not a modal: focus moves to its heading, not to Allow, and the thread stays reachable.
Resolved states are text, and an expiry is posted as a message in reading order.

dos.t: Do default anything that reaches people outside the workspace to Off.
Do show which permission made a step wait or skip, with a Change link.

donts.t: Don't hide permissions in settings only.
Don't treat silence as consent for risky actions.

components.name: Generated table columns and enrichment
components.summary: Add an AI column, test it on three rows, see the cost per row, then run it with progress and Stop. Each cell shows its own state and cites its record.
components.problem: Running a prompt across 1,000 rows is expensive and hard to undo, and wrong answers hide among right ones. Without a shared flow, each table runs AI differently and overwrites real data.
components.solution: Generated columns are separate from real data, carry the origin mark, and run on demand: test on a few rows first, show cost, then run with a progress bar and Stop. Cells fill one by one; failures say why; stale cells are marked out of date.

steps.t: Add a column from a short list ("Suggested title", "Risk of closing empty") or describe your own in the prompt editor, with fields from the row as removable chips.
Test on 3 rows before anything else; results appear in place for review.
Before running on all rows, show the cost per row and in total, and the number of rows.
Run fills cells one by one with a visible state (queued, writing, done, failed) and a progress bar with Stop.
A failed cell says why ("The listing has no description") with Try again; "Not found" means the model looked and found nothing; a dash means nothing to do.
When source data changes, mark the column out of date instead of rewriting it silently.

whenToUse.t: To add a judgement or summary to many rows at once in the data grid.

whenNotToUse.t: In the list table. Generated columns live only in the data grid.
To change real fields. A generated column never overwrites real data; applying a suggestion to a real field goes through Propose then apply.

guidelines.t: Default to testing when a run is expensive or affects many rows.
Show cost where the decision is made, on the Run button, in credits with the unit stated.
Each cell cites the record it used and shows when it was written.
Cells can be corrected one at a time or in bulk.
Runs keep a history so people can see and undo earlier runs.

content.t: Run button: "Run on 412 rows · about 412 credits".
Column header shows the origin mark and the time written: "Likely reason · 2 min ago".

accessibility.t: Cell states are text ("Writing", "Failed"), not only spinners or colours.

dos.t: Do test on a few rows first.
Do show cost before running.

donts.t: Don't auto-run a new column on every row.
Don't rewrite stale cells silently.

components.name: Saved tasks and schedules
components.summary: Turn repeated requests into a task sentence with editable slots, test it once, then save it and optionally run it on a schedule.
components.problem: Teams retype the same long prompt every Monday, with slightly different wording each time and different results. Scheduled automation that has never been tested surprises people.
components.solution: The task builder writes the task as a sentence with slots ("Find [Live listings] with [apply rate under 3%]..."). Slots reuse filter values. An empty slot blocks Run and says which one. Test runs once in the assistant; Save as task adds an optional schedule.

steps.t: Start from a template, a past answer ("Save as task") or a blank builder.
The task is a sentence with slots; slots reuse filter values and record pickers.
An empty slot is dashed and blocks Run, with a message naming it: "Choose who gets the titles before you run this."
Run once (⌘↵) to test. The result arrives as a normal answer with proposals.
Save as task, then optionally add a schedule ("Every Monday") and check the permissions the task will use.
Scheduled runs appear first in previous conversations, notify before changing anything, and wait in the Inbox when they need approval.

whenToUse.t: For tasks repeated with the same structure and different values: weekly reviews, renaming, chasing hiring managers.

whenNotToUse.t: For one-off questions; just ask.

guidelines.t: Slots are the parts that change; the rest of the sentence is fixed so results are consistent.
Keep slots few; too many raise effort and reduce quality.
A task must run successfully once before it can be scheduled.
Scheduled tasks use the same agent permissions, shown explicitly when the schedule is set; changes default to Ask first.
Picking a template opens it as a draft task, never runs it.

content.t: Tasks read as one sentence starting with a verb: "Find ..., then suggest ... and send them to ...".

accessibility.t: Each slot is a button with its field name and current value, and opens a popover with one field.
Empty required slots are announced with the error message, not only shown dashed.

dos.t: Do reuse filter values in slots.
Do test before scheduling.

donts.t: Don't save free prompts as scheduled tasks.
Don't let a schedule change records without a notice or approval.

components.name: Data visualisation
components.summary: Start from the question the person is asking, pick the one chart that answers it, give it a noun title, units and a period, and ship it with a table view and its four states.
components.problem: Hiring leads open dashboards to answer a few questions: is volume going up, did something break, how do teams compare, why did this week drop. When charts are picked for looks, or each team invents its own axis and colour habits, people misread them or stop trusting them.
components.solution: Name the objective first (trend, anomaly, comparison, investigation), then choose the chart from a fixed table, show the fewest series that answer it, and finish it the same way every time: noun title, period, one y-axis, colours in order, table view, accessible name and the four states.

steps.t: Write the question in one line, then tag it: trend over time, spotting something unusual, comparing groups, or investigating a known problem.

Choose the chart: change over time is a line; amounts per category or period are bars; parts of a total over time are a stacked area; two to five parts at one moment are a donut; ordered stages are a funnel; two measures across records are a scatter; one number is a stat card.
Show the fewest series that answer the question: up to eight lines or bars, four on a bar and line chart, five parts on a donut. Past that, fold into "Other" or add a series filter.
Finish the chart: noun title, period subtitle, axis titles with units, one y-axis, legend only for two or more series, categorical colours in order.
Add the table view and the accessible name and description.
Build the four states: loading, empty, no match and error.

whenToUse.t: Whenever a screen shows numbers that people read as a shape: trends, comparisons, splits.
On dashboards and report pages, and in a record's detail when history matters, such as applications per day for a listing.

whenNotToUse.t: For decoration or to fill space. If nobody acts on it, leave it out.
When the person needs exact values per record. Use the List table or Breakdown table.
When there is one number that matters. Use the Stat card with comparison.

guidelines.t: Never let the chart suggest something the data does not say. Bars and areas start at zero; a line that starts elsewhere says so on the axis.
Keep the number of charts per view small, and give charts of equal importance the same size.
A series keeps its colour on every chart on the page, and hiding a series never repaints the others.
Show gaps where data is missing. A missing day is not a zero.
When a chart has three or more series, offer a series filter; with one series, offer neither a filter nor a legend.
Thresholds are dashed, fixed lines with a text label, such as "Target 40". They are not a series and never use the status colours on their own.

content.t: Titles are nouns that name the measure: "Applications", "Time to first reply". Never "Chart 1" or a sentence about the result.
Axis titles are one to three words with the unit: "Salary (£k)". Time axes need no title; the dates speak for themselves.
Dates on axes are short and UK style: "3 Nov", "Mon", "Nov". Currency carries its symbol: "£32k".

State copy follows TwoUX's states pattern: "Loading applications", "No applications in this period", "No data matches these filters" with Clear filters, and "Couldn't load applications" with Try again.
Use "previous" and "following", not "above" and "below", and "select", not "click".

accessibility.t: Give every chart an accessible name matching its visible title and a description in the form "[Chart type] showing [data], [period]."
Every chart has a Table view with the same values; it is the long description and the fallback for anyone who reads tables more easily.
Colour is never the only cue: series have names in the tooltip and direct labels, groups have shapes or line styles.
Marks needed to read the data reach 3:1 against the background; text uses text colours, never the series colour.
The plot, legend and popover are reachable by keyboard in a logical order, and pinned popovers stay until dismissed.

dos.t: Do start from the question and name it in the chart title.
Do ship a Table view with every chart.
Do split two units into two charts side by side.

donts.t: Don't add a second y-axis.
Don't colour each bar of a single series differently.
Don't use a donut for change over time or for more than five parts.
Don't print values or labels in the series colour.

components.name: Chart drill-down
components.summary: Select a point on a chart to see what makes it up, then narrow the chart or the whole page to that point, with every applied filter shown as a pill you can remove.
components.problem: A hiring lead sees applications drop on 12 Oct and wants to know why. Without a way in from the chart, they rebuild the same filters by hand on another page and lose the thread.
components.solution: Offer three levels and pick one per chart. A breakdown in the details popover answers most questions. If more is needed, a footer in the pinned popover filters either this chart or the whole page, never both on one page. Filters land as pills in the filter bar, write to the URL and come off with one click.

steps.t: Hover or move the crosshair to a point; the details popover shows each series' value. Select it or press Enter to pin the popover.
Breakdown: under a value, list up to seven parts that make it up, such as applications on 12 Oct by listing. More than seven ends with a link: "View all 14 in table".
Link either the part's name to its record or its value to a filtered List table, never both.
Chart drill-down: the popover footer has a title saying where the filter goes ("Filter this chart"), the chosen point as read-only values ("Date 12 Oct"), an optional select ("Team"), and one button.
Page drill-down: the same footer, titled "Filter this page", applies the values to the page's filter bar so every chart and table updates.
Every applied value appears as a pill ("Date is 12 Oct") and in the URL, so Clear filters, removing a pill or Back returns to the default view.

whenToUse.t: When people look at charts to investigate: a spike, a drop or an outlier they need to explain.
Page drill-down on dashboards where several charts and a table share filters, such as a hiring overview by team and location.

whenNotToUse.t: Do not mix chart drill-down and page drill-down on the same page. Pick one; two levels of filters conflict.
For a chart with one series and nothing beneath it. The tooltip is enough.
On a Board item people rearrange: send them to the full report page instead of filtering inside a tile.

guidelines.t: Always say which filters a drill-down will apply and where, before it runs.
Pre-filled values from the selected point are read-only in the popover; only the optional extra choice is editable.
Filtering is a reversible view change, so it needs no confirmation and no Undo toast: the pill and Back undo it.
A pinned popover follows Popover rules: one open at a time, never cut off, Esc closes it and returns focus to the point.
Popover footers hold at most two buttons; more go in a menu.
The popover breakdown is never the only place a value lives. The Breakdown table under the chart holds the same split.

content.t: Footer title names the target: "Filter this chart" or "Filter this page". Description lists what will apply: "Date is 12 Oct and Team is Design."
Button names the action and target: "Filter chart", "Filter page". Not "Apply" or "Submit".
Breakdown rows read as key and value: "Junior Product Designer, Leeds  18".

accessibility.t: Enter on a focused point pins the popover; Tab moves through its links, select and button; Esc closes it and returns focus to the same point.
The popover is labelled by the point it describes: "Applications, 12 Oct".
After a drill-down applies, announce the new state politely: "Filtered to 12 Oct. 3 charts updated."
Read-only values are text, not disabled inputs, so they are read in full and not skipped.

dos.t: Do show every drill-down filter as a pill in the filter bar.
Do cap a popover breakdown at seven items with a link to the rest.
Do keep the drill-down state in the URL.

donts.t: Don't offer chart and page drill-down on the same page.
Don't link both the name and the value in a breakdown row.
Don't apply filters from a hover; only from a pinned popover and a button.

components.name: Static dashboard
components.summary: A fixed overview page where the team sees the same items in the same order, most important first, answering the day's questions at a glance.
components.problem: A hiring lead opens the overview to answer a few questions fast: how many applications came in, which listings need attention, what is stuck. If the page is a wall of charts, or each team lays it out differently, the answer takes minutes instead of seconds.
components.solution: Lay the page out in three bands on a 12-column grid: a top band with page actions and the headline numbers, a middle band of charts and short lists that explain those numbers, and a bottom band for setup help and updates. The order is set by the product team from research and does not change per person.

steps.t: Write down the three to five questions the page must answer, such as "Are applications up or down this week?" and "Which listings expire in the next 7 days?". Every item must answer one of them.
Top band: the page header with page-level actions (period control, Post a listing) and a row of up to four key metrics with comparisons.
Middle band: charts and short lists that give the context behind the key metrics, such as applications per week and candidates waiting over 5 days.
Bottom band: getting started help for new workspaces, and short notes on product updates with a link to read more.
Size items from the 12-column grid: 3 columns for a small item, 6 for medium, 9 for large, 12 for full width. Height follows the content.
Give every item a way out to the full view ("View all 23 listings") so the dashboard stays a summary.

whenToUse.t: For a team-wide overview where everyone should see the same numbers in the same order, such as the weekly hiring report shared with department heads.
When the order of items matters to getting the job done, for example during a hiring campaign where the funnel must stay in view.
As the default home of a workspace before you know enough about how people want to rearrange it.

whenNotToUse.t: When people in different roles need different items, such as a recruiter watching their own pipeline and a lead watching cost per hire. Use the configurable dashboard.
To browse, filter or edit records. Link to the List table instead of embedding a full table.
For a single metric explored in depth. Give it its own report page with a chart and a Breakdown table.

guidelines.t: Keep to about seven items on one dashboard and about seven series or rows inside any one item. If you need more, split into a parent overview and child dashboards, such as one per department.
Decide whether the page is operational (what needs action today) or analytical (trends over months). A mix is fine, but put the operational items first.
Page-level controls change every item at once and always have a value, so the period uses a segmented control or dropdown, not a filter pill.
Each item loads, fails and shows empty on its own. One failed chart shows an error state in its card; the rest of the page still works.
Design the narrow layout too: on a phone the bands stack into one column in priority order, and dense charts are replaced by their headline number and a link to the full chart.
Make the dashboard the first link in the side navigation when it is the landing page for returning users.

content.t: Item titles name what is measured and the scope: "Applications this week", "Listings expiring in 7 days".
Every number says what it compares against, using the Comparison over time pattern: "+12% vs previous 7 days".
Use "previous" and "following", not "above" and "below": the layout stacks differently on narrow screens.
Update notes are one sentence and a link, such as "You can now schedule the weekly hiring report. Set up a schedule".

accessibility.t: The page has one h1; each item title is an h2 and any sub-heading inside an item is an h3, so screen reader users can jump between items by heading.
Focus order follows the visual order, band by band and left to right.
Every chart has its data available as a table (the Chart or Table switch) and a text summary of the headline.
Status in items is a word in a badge, never colour alone.

dos.t: Do put the item that answers the most frequent question in the first row.
Do link each item to the page where the work happens.
Do show the time the data was last updated in the page header.

donts.t: Don't show long lists such as activity logs; show the top five and link to the rest.
Don't put complex filtering inside items. Send people to the list or report page for that.
Don't mix fixed items and movable items on one page.

components.name: Configurable dashboard
components.summary: A personal overview where each person adds, removes, moves and resizes items on a board, with an items palette to add from, a saved layout and a reset to the default.
