components.problem: Recruiters, hiring managers and the head of talent watch different things. One fixed overview is either too crowded for each of them or missing what one of them needs, so they build their own spreadsheets instead.
components.solution: Start from the static dashboard layout as the default, then let each person change it on a Board. Add items opens the items palette in a side panel; items move by drag, keyboard or menu; Remove is undoable and puts the item back in the palette; the layout is saved per person and Reset to default layout brings back the original.

steps.t: Build the default layout first with the static dashboard guidelines; this is what new people see and what Reset returns to.
Put Add items in the page header. It opens the items palette in a side panel that pushes the board, and closes with the same button or Esc.
People add an item by dragging it from the palette onto the board, or by choosing Add to dashboard on the palette item, which places it at the end of the board and moves focus to it.
People move and resize items by dragging the handles, by keyboard on the handle, or from the item menu (Move earlier, Move later, Wider, Narrower, Taller, Shorter).
Remove from dashboard is the last entry in the item menu. It removes at once, shows a toast with Undo, and the item reappears in the palette.
Save every change to the person's layout on the server as it happens; there is no Save button.
Reset to default layout sits in the page header's more menu. It applies at once and offers Undo in a toast.

whenToUse.t: For a personal home page where people in different roles need different items, such as "My open listings" for a recruiter and "Cost per hire" for the head of talent.
When there are more useful items than fit on one screen, and each person only needs some of them.
When people use the page for investigation and want related items side by side.

whenNotToUse.t: For a shared report that must read the same for everyone. Use the static dashboard.
When there are fewer than about six possible items. Rearranging adds work and little value; fix the layout instead.
Inside a side panel or dialog. The board is the main content of its page.

guidelines.t: Make the whole page configurable or none of it. Don't pin some items in place among movable ones.
Moving an item keeps its size, its settings and what it shows, such as the period or the location it is set to.
Show a drop preview the size and shape of the item while dragging. Items swap when there is room and push others along when there is not; a drop outside the board puts the item back.
The board has 4 columns on wide screens, 2 on tablets and 1 on phones. Store one layout per column count, so a change on a laptop doesn't scramble the phone layout.
Layouts are personal. Changing yours never changes a colleague's dashboard or the workspace default.
When the board is empty, show an empty state with Add items and Reset to default layout.

content.t: Header actions: "Add items" and, in the more menu, "Reset to default layout".
Removal toast names the item: "Removed Applications this week. Undo".
Reset toast: "Dashboard reset to the default layout. Undo".
Empty board: "Your dashboard has no items" with "Add items to see your hiring numbers here."

accessibility.t: Dragging is never the only way: every add, move and resize also works by keyboard and from a menu or button with a single pointer action.
Announce each pick-up, move, resize, drop, add and removal in a polite live region, naming the item and its new position: "Applications this week moved to row 1, column 2".
After Add to dashboard, move focus to the new item's handle; after Remove, move focus to the next item, or to Add items if the board is now empty.
Drag and resize handles have names that include the item title: "Move Applications this week", "Resize Applications this week".

dos.t: Do return a removed item to the palette so it can be added again.
Do keep Remove and Add items close in meaning and in place: one undoes the other.
Do keep the layout the person made on their next visit and on any device with the same column count.

donts.t: Don't ask for confirmation before removing an item; offer Undo.
Don't show a banner inside the board after a removal. The toast is enough.
Don't store the layout only in the browser; it is lost on another device or after clearing data.

components.name: Dashboard items
components.summary: The catalogue of item types a dashboard is built from, such as key metrics, charts, short lists, alerts, quick links, getting started and feature news, and what each one should contain.
components.problem: Without a shared catalogue, every new dashboard item invents its own header, actions and amount of data. Items grow into mini reports with their own filters and tables, and the dashboard stops being readable at a glance.
components.solution: Every item is a board item with the same anatomy: title, optional description, at most one header action, a more menu, content, and an optional footer link. The content is one of a small set of types, each with a clear job and size, and each links to the page where the full data lives.

steps.t: Key metrics (full width): two to four Stat cards with comparison, such as Live listings, Applications this week, Median days to first review, Offers accepted. Each opens its report.
Chart (medium or large): one chart that explains a key metric, such as applications per week or the views to offers funnel, with the Chart or Table switch and a View report link.
List or table (medium or large): the top five records that need attention, such as listings expiring in 7 days or candidates waiting over 5 days, with status badges and "View all 23" in the footer.
Status and alerts (small or full width): what is wrong now and what to do, such as "Indeed sync failed for 2 listings" with Retry sync. It shows "No issues" when all is well rather than disappearing.
Quick links and resources (small): three to five links to frequent destinations or help, such as Post a listing, Import candidates, Interview scorecard guide.
Getting started (medium): the workspace setup checklist for new teams, with progress such as "2 of 5 done". People can dismiss it once they are set up.
Feature news (small): one product update in a sentence with one link. It is dismissible, and there is never more than one on a dashboard.

whenToUse.t: Whenever you add anything to a static or configurable dashboard: pick a type from this catalogue first.
When a summary can be read on its own without the other items.
When the item has a clear destination for people who need more detail.

whenNotToUse.t: For data people need to filter, sort and act on in bulk. Link to the List table.
For long text or logs, such as the full activity history of a listing. Put it on the record page.
For a single number with no comparison and no action. Fold it into the key metrics row or leave it out.

guidelines.t: One item, one job. Combine at most two visual types in an item, such as a chart with its breakdown table, never a chart, a table and a list.

At most one action in the header, for the most common next step. Everything else goes in the more menu: Preferences first, then other actions by how often they are used, then Remove from dashboard last.
Show all the content by default. Preferences can hide parts, such as a column or the table under a chart, but only on configurable dashboards.
Keep the content light: no inline filters beyond a period or one select, no row selection, no editing. Link out for anything more.
Size by content: small (1 of 4 columns) for one number or a few links, medium (2) for a chart or short list, large (3) for a chart that compares several series, full width (4) for key metrics.
An AI summary item, if offered, carries the origin label, cites the records it used by ID and only suggests. It never ranks, rejects or advances candidates.
Give each item's title heading level 2 (level={2} on ChartFrame, BoardItem and ChangeList) so the page outline runs from the h1 straight to the items and screen reader users can jump between them.

content.t: Title is a noun phrase with scope: "Candidates waiting over 5 days", not "Waiting" or "Widget 3".
Footer links say how many: "View all 23 listings", not "See more".
Item menu labels are verbs or plain nouns: "Preferences", "View report", "Remove from dashboard".
An item with nothing to show explains why and what to do: "No listings expire in the next 7 days."

accessibility.t: Each item is a region labelled by its h2 title.
Key metric changes are read as words: "Up 12% vs previous 7 days", not only an arrow and a colour.
A table inside a narrow item scrolls inside the item, not the page, and keeps its header row.
Alerts that appear after load are announced politely; failures that block work use the error state in the item.

dos.t: Do treat each item as an executive summary of its subject.
Do give every list and chart item a link to its full page.
Do keep loading, empty and error states inside the item's frame so the layout does not jump.

donts.t: Don't add actions that belong on another page, such as Post a listing inside a chart item.
Don't use expanding footers or accordions inside items.
Don't show more than one feature news item, and never one that cannot be dismissed.

components.name: Regenerating an answer
components.summary: Regenerate reruns the same question with the same context and replaces the latest answer, keeping the earlier version one step away. It never touches changes already applied.
components.problem: The first answer sometimes takes the wrong angle: too long, the wrong listings, the wrong period. Typing "try again" sends a new message, so the thread fills with near-duplicates and the assistant reads the bad answer as context.
components.solution: Put a Regenerate button in the answer actions of the latest answer. It reruns the original question with the same context chips and settings, and the new answer takes the old one's place with a "2 / 2" switch to go back. It works the same after a finished answer and after Stop.

steps.t: While the assistant works, the send button becomes Stop. Stop acts at once and keeps what was written so far, marked "Stopped".
Under the latest answer, finished or stopped, show Regenerate in the answer actions next to Copy and feedback.
Regenerate sends the same question with the same context chips, team files and Quick or Thorough setting. Nothing new is typed into the thread.
The new answer replaces the old one in place. A "2 / 2" control under it switches between versions; the thread continues from the version on screen.
If regenerating fails, keep the earlier version on screen and show the error under it with Try again.

whenToUse.t: When the person asked a question and wants a different take on the same request, such as a shorter summary of why LST-1044 has few applicants.
After Stop, when the answer was heading the wrong way and the question itself was fine.
For drafts the person will review anyway, such as a job description or an interview question set.

whenNotToUse.t: To change the question. Edit the question or send a new message; regenerate repeats the input exactly.
On agent runs or scheduled tasks that changed data. Run them again as a new run under the same permissions.
On a single generated table cell. Use Try again on the cell (see Generated table columns).

guidelines.t: Offer Regenerate on the latest answer only. Regenerating an earlier answer would drop everything after it, which the person can't see coming.
Only answers the person asked for get Regenerate. Starters, notices and approval results don't.
Regenerating never undoes or repeats applied changes. Changes already applied stay applied; reversing them is Undo's job.
Suggested changes in the replaced version are dropped if not yet applied; the new version brings its own proposal.
Each version keeps its own citations and origin label, so switching versions never mixes sources.

content.t: Button tooltip and accessible name: "Regenerate answer". Version control: "2 / 2", with "Previous version" and "Next version" as names.
A stopped answer ends with "Stopped" in muted text, not an apology.
Failure: "Couldn't regenerate. Your earlier answer is still here." then Try again.

accessibility.t: Regenerate sits in the answer actions, which follow the answer in tab order, so it is reached right after reading.
Focus stays on Regenerate while the new answer is written; announce "Regenerating" and then the finished answer once.
The version switch announces the version on screen: "Version 1 of 2".

dos.t: Do let people stop at once and regenerate straight after.
Do keep the earlier version reachable.
Do keep the same context chips for the rerun, visibly.

donts.t: Don't put a confirmation or delay on Stop.
Don't show Regenerate on every answer in the thread.
Don't let regenerate reverse or repeat applied changes.

components.name: Generated drafts and files
components.summary: Show what the assistant makes (a job description, a CSV, a chart) as a card under the answer. Short things are read and copied in place; long drafts open on the assistant page. Anything that would change a record goes through Suggested changes.
components.problem: Hiring teams ask the assistant for things they will use elsewhere: a job description for a new role, a CSV of expiring listings, a chart of applications by week. Pasted into the answer text, these are hard to copy, easy to lose and easy to mistake for saved data.
components.solution: Each output becomes a generated file card stacked under the answer, with name, type, size and origin label, and its own actions. Short, self-contained output stays inline. Long drafts open beside the conversation on the assistant page. Saving a draft into a listing is a suggested change the person applies.

steps.t: When an answer produces something to keep, place it as a card below the answer text, one card per output, never inside a paragraph.
Choose inline or open by length and intent: a short snippet, a CSV or a chart image stays inline with Copy or Download; a full job description opens to read and edit.
Open shows the draft on the assistant page in the Answer area, with the conversation still beside it.
If the draft belongs on a record (the description of LST-1044), the card's main action is "Suggest for LST-1044", which adds it to Suggested changes with before and after.
Applying works like every proposal: step card, toast with Undo.

whenToUse.t: For drafts people will edit or reuse: job descriptions, interview question sets, rejection email drafts for a recruiter to send themselves.
For files to download: CSV of listings, a chart as PNG.
For a chart the assistant drew from listings data, shown inline with Download and a data table on Open.

whenNotToUse.t: For a figure or a short table that answers the question. Keep it in the answer.
For direct edits to a record field. Use Suggested changes.
For exports of a table view. Use the Export menu on the table.

guidelines.t: Keep file actions in the card and answer actions in the answer row, so Copy on the card copies the file and Copy under the answer copies the answer.
Two visible actions at most on a card; the rest go in a More menu.
Every card carries the origin label and the records it drew on, as the answer does.
A draft is never saved anywhere until the person downloads, copies or applies it. Say so on the card.
Drafts about candidates are for a person to review and send. The assistant never sends or decides on its own.

content.t: Card title is the file name or what it is: "Job description, Junior Product Designer", "expiring-listings.csv".
Metadata uses standard units and plain types: "CSV · 14 KB · 38 rows".
Main action verbs: "Open", "Download", "Copy", "Suggest for LST-1044".

accessibility.t: Each card is a group named by its title; its actions are named with the file, such as "Download expiring-listings.csv".
Generated charts include a text summary and the data as a table on Open.
Opening a draft moves focus to its heading; closing returns focus to the card.

dos.t: Do stack each output in its own card under the answer.
Do route record changes through Suggested changes.
Do show size and row counts before download.

donts.t: Don't nest file cards inside answer text.
Don't put a Save to record button on a draft.
Don't mix file actions into the answer actions row.

components.name: Asking for details inside the answer
components.summary: When the assistant knows what to do but needs a few values to do it, it asks with a short form card in the thread, prefilled from context. Submitting the form produces a proposal, not a change.
components.problem: Some requests need specific values before anything can be prepared: "Draft a new listing like LST-1044 for Manchester" needs a salary band and a closing date. Asking in prose makes people type values in free text, which the assistant then has to parse and may get wrong.
components.solution: Show an input card in the conversation with only the required fields, at most five, prefilled with what can be inferred and a line saying why the values are needed. Completed cards collapse to a read-only summary with Edit. The result is a Suggested changes card the person applies.

steps.t: Ask only once the intent is clear. If it isn't, use the clarifying question card first.
Show one card per thing being set up, titled after it: "Closing date and salary for the Manchester listing".
Prefill from context: location from the request, salary band from the team file, closing date from the usual 30 days. Mark what was prefilled and from where.
Steps that depend on each other appear one at a time; independent ones appear together as separate cards that can be done in any order.
On Continue, the card collapses to a summary line with Edit, and the assistant prepares the proposal from the values.

whenToUse.t: When an action needs values with a known shape: dates, locations, salary bands, a choice of listing.
When the person must check a value the assistant chose before it is used, shown as an editable field with an edit icon.
When an agent run reaches a step that needs one value from the person, such as which listings to include.

whenNotToUse.t: To find out what the person means. Use the clarifying question card with options.
For long setup with many fields, such as creating a listing from scratch. Open the listing form instead.
For decisions about candidates. The assistant does not collect inputs to decide on people.

guidelines.t: Five fields at most, all required. If a field is optional, leave it out.
Say why the values are needed in one line above the fields.
Use the same inputs as the rest of TwoUX: date picker for dates, select for known lists. Validate on Continue like any form.
Never ask for something the workspace already holds; prefill it instead.
A card left unanswered doesn't block the thread: the composer stays usable and the card can be dismissed.

content.t: Card titles name the thing, not the need: "Closing date for LST-1061", not "Information required".
Prefill note: "From team file Salary bands 2026".
Collapsed summary: "Manchester · £28,000 to £32,000 · closes 6 Dec" then Edit.

accessibility.t: When the card appears, announce it and move focus to its heading, not to the first field or Continue.
The card is not a dialog and doesn't trap focus; the thread and composer stay reachable.
Each field has a visible label; prefilled values are announced with their source.

dos.t: Do prefill from context and say where values came from.
Do collapse completed cards to a summary with Edit.
Do turn the values into a proposal the person applies.

donts.t: Don't ask for optional fields.
Don't use a form to clarify intent.
Don't show several dependent steps at once.

components.name: Agent activity log
components.summary: A chronological list of what agents and the assistant did across runs: time, an icon with a word for the outcome, a past-tense label that links to the run or message, grouped by day.
components.problem: A single run shows its own steps, but people ask broader questions: what did the listings agent do this week, which run changed LST-1044, when did someone approve that. Without a log they search through conversations and inbox items from memory.
components.solution: An activity log on each agent and on the assistant page lists events in time order, newest last within each day, grouped under Today, Yesterday and dated dividers. Each event has a time, a status icon with a word, and a past-tense label that opens the run step, message or record it refers to. A filter narrows by agent, event type or outcome.

steps.t: Group events by day with a labelled divider: Today, Yesterday, then dates such as "Tue 4 Nov 2026".
Each row: time in a fixed-width column, outcome icon with a word, a past-tense label, and who started it.
The label links to where it happened: the run step, the conversation message or the record.
Filter by agent, event type (read, changed, waited, failed) or outcome using the filter bar.
On a long conversation, the assistant page can show the same list as an outline whose rows jump to each message.

whenToUse.t: On each agent's detail to answer "what did it do and when".
On a long task conversation, as an outline to move between key moments.
When someone needs to trace which run changed a listing, for example during a review of closing dates.

whenNotToUse.t: While a single run is in progress. Use the agent run timeline with its live steps and Stop.
For a record's own change history. Use the record's history, which also shows changes people made.
As a notification feed. Things that need someone go to the Inbox.

guidelines.t: Every event an agent took is in the log: what it read, changed, waited for and failed, with who started the run.
Use the same step states and icons as the run timeline; outcome is a word plus an icon, never colour alone.
Mark events a person did differently from agent events, with the person's avatar, so approvals and rejections stand out.
Omit the time column where the label already links to a timestamped message.
Don't auto-scroll to new events unless the person is already at the end of the list.

content.t: Agent events in the past tense: "Changed closing date on LST-1044", "Read 9 listings".
Person events start with the verb: "Approved 2 changes", "Rejected sending to Leeds team".
Times in the person's local time, with the full date and time on hover.

accessibility.t: Day groups are lists with a heading each, so screen reader users can jump by day.
New events in an open log are announced politely, at most once every few seconds.
Outcome icons have text equivalents; the word is visible, not only in a tooltip.

dos.t: Do link every event to where it happened.
Do group by day once activity spans dates.
Do mark events people did with their avatar.

donts.t: Don't pull people to the bottom while they read older events.
Don't leave out failed or skipped events to make the log look tidy.
Don't show a time column when the label already links to a timestamped message.

components.name: Managing agents
components.summary: One Agents page lists every agent with its source, what it does, whether it is on and where it may act. People turn agents on and off with Undo, edit scope in the side panel, and agents are never switched off or deleted without someone choosing to.
components.problem: As a team adds agents (a listings checker, a scheduler, a third-party sourcing tool), nobody can see in one place which are on, who added them, what they can reach and which listings they touch. Trust drops when an agent acts somewhere people didn't expect.
components.solution: An Agents page with a list table: name and avatar, source, short description, capabilities as tags, scope, status as a word badge and an On switch. Selecting a row opens the agent in the side panel with its permissions, scope and activity log. Add agent sits in the page header.

steps.t: List agents in a table with name, source (TwoUX, your team, or the third party that provides it), what it does, scope, owner and status.
Turn an agent on or off with its switch. The change applies at once with a toast and Undo; runs in progress finish or stop as the person chooses.
Open a row to see and edit its permissions per action, its scope (which teams, listings or locations) and its activity log.
Add agent opens the templates gallery or connected tools; a new agent starts Off with changes set to Ask first.
If an agent can't run (a connection expired), mark it "Needs attention" and send its owner an Inbox item. Don't switch it off.

whenToUse.t: When a workspace has more than one agent, or any agent from a third party.
To answer "what can act on our listings, and who said it could".
When an admin reviews access, for example before a new team joins the workspace.

whenNotToUse.t: To set what one agent may do in a single run. Use the permission card in the run (Ask first, Allow).
For outside tools the assistant can read from. Use Connected tools.
For saved tasks a person runs themselves. Those live in Saved tasks.

guidelines.t: Show the source next to the name so people can judge trust before turning an agent on.
Permissions and scope are visible on the page and editable in place, never only inside a setup flow.
Never switch off or delete an agent automatically. Failures are reported, not acted on.
Actions that decide on candidates (reject, advance, score for shortlisting) can't be set to Allow for any agent; they stay with a person.
Deleting an agent removes its schedule but keeps its activity log. It is irreversible, so it uses the confirmation dialog.

content.t: Page title "Agents" with one line: "Agents that can read or change your hiring data, and where."
Status words: On, Off, Needs attention. Capability tags are verbs: "Reads listings", "Suggests closing dates".
Button: "Add agent".

accessibility.t: Each switch is named with the agent: "Turn on Listings checker".
Status is a word in a badge, so it reads without colour.
The switch change and its Undo are announced as a status message.

dos.t: Do show source, scope and status at a glance.
Do start new agents Off with changes on Ask first.
Do let people edit scope from the row's side panel.

donts.t: Don't auto-disable or delete an agent.
Don't let any agent be allowed to decide on candidates.
Don't hide permissions inside the setup flow.

components.name: Disabled and read-only states
components.summary: Show an action as unavailable only when the person can do something about it, say why in one sentence, and show values they can't change as read-only rather than greyed out.
components.problem: A greyed-out button with no explanation leaves people guessing whether it is broken, waiting for something, or forbidden. Greyed-out fields are hard to read, and a disabled Save button hides which field is the problem.
components.solution: Pick one of three treatments. Hide what this person can never use. Disable, with a one-sentence reason, what they could use once something changes. Make read-only what they need to see but not change. Submit buttons are never disabled.

steps.t: Ask whether this person could ever use the control. If their role never can, such as a Viewer and Billing settings, hide it.
If they could once something changes (select rows, publish the listing, ask the owner), show it as unavailable and give the reason.
Put a short reason in a tooltip on the button, menu item, tab or option. Put a longer reason, or one with a next step, in text or a banner beside the control.

For values that are shown but not editable, such as a listing's ID or a field locked by the job board feed, use the read-only state: normal text colour, no input border, still selectable and copyable.
On a review step where nothing is editable, show plain text values instead of read-only inputs.

whenToUse.t: Disabled: Close listing in the bulk bar while one of the selected listings is still a draft.
Disabled: Publish on a listing whose owner is someone else and the person is an Editor without publish rights.
Read-only: the salary band on a listing approved by finance, shown in the edit form so people know what will be published.

whenNotToUse.t: On a form's submit button. Keep it enabled and let pressing it show what is missing (see Inline editing and validation).
For actions this person's role can never have. Hide them; a wall of disabled items is noise.
To stop a reversible action that is merely risky. Let it run and offer Undo.

guidelines.t: Use aria-disabled, not the HTML disabled attribute, on any control that carries a reason, so it stays focusable and keyboard users can reach the reason.
A disabled control keeps its place and size; it does not jump or vanish when the state changes.
Reasons are plain text only. No links or buttons inside a tooltip reason; if the next step needs a link, use a banner or helper text.
Only give a reason when the label and context don't already make it obvious. An unavailable Delete with nothing selected needs none.
Read-only fields are still part of the form's data and its tab order, so screen reader users hear the value.
Unavailable is never shown by colour alone: the control also loses its hover state and announces as unavailable.

content.t: Permission reason: "Only the listing owner can publish. Ask Priya Shah to publish it."
Waiting on something: "Available when the listing is Live." or "Available when you select a listing."
System limit: "Unavailable while the job board feed is syncing." Say what is happening, not "Error".
One sentence for the reason, an optional second for the next step. No "please", no exclamation marks.

accessibility.t: Unavailable controls use aria-disabled="true", stay in the tab order, and ignore activation; the tooltip reason is linked with aria-describedby.
Disabled text is exempt from contrast minimums, but TwoUX keeps it at 3:1 so it can still be read.
Read-only inputs use the readonly attribute (or aria-readonly in a grid), never aria-disabled.
Tooltip reasons appear on focus as well as hover and can be dismissed with Esc.

dos.t: Do say what makes the action available.
Do hide controls a role can never use.
Do show locked values as readable text, not faded inputs.

donts.t: Don't disable a form's submit button to signal missing fields.
Don't put links or buttons inside a disabled reason tooltip.
Don't use the native disabled attribute on a control that has a reason; keyboard users can't reach the tooltip.

components.name: Drag and drop
components.summary: Dragging is a shortcut, never the only way: every drag in TwoUX has a keyboard path and a menu path that do the same thing.
components.problem: Dragging is quick for some people and impossible for others, including keyboard, switch and tremor users. Drags without a visible handle go unnoticed, and drops that land somewhere unexpected move a candidate to the wrong stage.
components.solution: Mark draggable things with a handle, show where the item will land while it moves, and send an invalid drop back to where it started. Offer the same move from the keyboard (pick up, arrows, drop) and from a menu item such as Move to stage.

steps.t: Decide whether the drag is a shortcut (reordering columns, uploading a CV by dropping it) or the main way to do the task (arranging a dashboard). Main-way drags need the strongest signifiers and alternatives.
Give each draggable item a 16px grip handle in a 24px target, and change the cursor to grab on hover; resize handles use the matching resize cursor.
While dragging, lift the item with a shadow and show a drop preview the size of the item where it will land.
If the drop target is not allowed, show it as unavailable during the drag and return the item to its start on release.

After a drop, confirm the result in place and in a toast with Undo, unless the move is irreversible (such as moving a candidate to Rejected, which emails them); that opens a confirmation dialog first.

whenToUse.t: Reordering things whose order matters: pipeline stages, columns in the Columns menu, dashboard items on a board.
Moving a candidate card between stages on a pipeline board, alongside the Move to stage menu.
Dropping files, such as a CV or a job description document, onto an upload area that also has a Choose file button.

whenNotToUse.t: For sorting a table. Use sortable column headers; order there comes from the data, not from the person.
For bulk moves of many records. Select them and use the bulk action bar.
As the only way to do anything (WCAG 2.5.7).

guidelines.t: Every drag has a single-pointer alternative: arrow buttons or menu items such as Move up, Move down, Move to stage.
Every drag has a keyboard path: Tab to the handle, Enter or Space to pick up, arrows to move, Enter to drop, Esc to cancel.
Items of equal size swap places; otherwise the moving item pushes the others along. Never let items overlap.
Moves save per person or per team as the context says, and the result is visible at once: no Save button for a reorder.
Scroll the list or board automatically when the dragged item nears its edge.
Respect reduced motion: drop items into place without the slide animation.

Show every stage of a drag. Ready: the grip darkens on hover and focus, with a grab cursor and a tooltip saying how to move it. Dragging: a lifted copy follows the pointer, the board tints to show where drops are allowed, and a dashed slot shows exactly where the item will land.

Other items glide to make room (180ms, off with reduced motion) instead of jumping. On drop, a short highlight settles on the moved item and the new position is announced. Esc cancels and puts it back.

content.t: Handle accessible name: "Move Junior Product Designer", with a description of the keys.
Live announcements say position in words: "Picked up Interview. Stage 3 of 6." then "Interview moved to stage 2 of 6."
Upload area text names both paths: "Drop a CV here or choose a file".

accessibility.t: Dragging is never the only way to move, reorder or resize (2.5.7 Dragging Movements).
Handles meet the 24 by 24px target size (2.5.8).
Pick-up, each move, drop and cancel are announced in a polite live region (4.1.3).
Esc cancels and returns the item and focus to where they started.

dos.t: Do show a drop preview where the item will land.
Do offer the same move as a menu item.
Do use the same handle icon for every drag in the product.

donts.t: Don't make a whole row draggable with no handle; it fights text selection and click to open.
Don't drop silently into an invalid place; send the item back.
Don't trigger an email to a candidate from a drop without confirming first.

components.name: Error messages
components.summary: Put every error where it happened, at the smallest scope that contains it, and say what went wrong and what to do next in plain words.
components.problem: Errors shown far from their cause, raw API text, and messages that blame the person or promise help that never comes all erode trust. When one chart fails and the whole page goes blank, people lose work they could have kept doing.
components.solution: Match the place to the scope: a field error under the field, a form error in a banner above the form actions, a failed region in an error state that replaces only that region, a failed page in a page-level error state. Every message has a cause if known and a next step.

steps.t: Find the smallest scope that contains the failure: one field, one form, one region (a chart card, the side panel, a table), or the whole page.
Field: message under the field. Form or server error with no field: banner above the form's buttons. Region: error state in place of that region only. Page: error state in place of the page content.
For an action that failed after the person left the screen, such as an export or a bulk close, put a banner on the page they are on and an Inbox item; never a toast that fades.
Write the message: what happened, why if known, what to do now. Add Try again when retrying could work.
Put technical detail (request ID, error code) in a collapsed Details section the person can copy into a support request.

whenToUse.t: Any time something failed and the person needs to know: a value is invalid, a save failed, data didn't load, an action was refused.
Unexpected crashes in one part of the page: wrap each region in an error boundary so the rest stays usable.
When an action partly worked, such as a bulk close where some listings were already closed by someone else.

whenNotToUse.t: For warnings or advice, such as a salary below the advertised range for similar roles. Use a warning banner or field warning; errors mean something must be fixed now.
For a list that loaded fine and is empty. Use the empty state.
For a reversible action that worked. Use a toast.

guidelines.t: Use the built-in error state of a component (a combobox that failed to load options, a chart that failed to fetch) before inventing a new one.
Errors never auto-dismiss. A failed save stays visible until it succeeds or the person dismisses it.
Keep what the person entered. A failed submit leaves every field filled and stays on the page until the result is known.
Show the count when it helps: "3 of 12 listings couldn't be closed", with a link that filters to those three.
Never claim the team has been told unless errors really are reported automatically.
Report unexpected errors to the error tracker with the request ID shown in Details, so a support request can be matched.

content.t: Pattern: what happened, then what to do. "Couldn't save the closing date. Check your connection and try again."
Don't blame: "Enter a closing date after today", not "You entered an invalid date".
Plain words over codes: "This listing was changed by Tom Reid while you were editing" rather than "409 Conflict".
No "Oops", no jokes, no exclamation marks, no "sorry" in every message.

accessibility.t: Errors are text and an icon, never colour alone.
Field errors link to their field with aria-describedby and set aria-invalid.
A banner that appears after submit moves focus to itself, or to the first field in error; a region error is announced as a status without stealing focus.
Suggest the fix when it is known (3.3.3).

dos.t: Do keep the failure inside the region that failed.
Do offer Try again when a retry could work.
Do keep the person's input after any failure.

donts.t: Don't show raw API or stack trace text as the main message.
Don't report a failure in a toast that disappears after 6 seconds.
Don't use red error styling for a warning.

components.name: Contextual help
components.summary: Answer "what is this, why does it matter, how do I choose" in three steps of depth: the words on the screen, a help panel opened from an Info link, and a help centre article in a new tab.
components.problem: Help that lives only in a separate help centre isn't found at the moment of need, and help crammed into the page as long descriptions slows everyone down. Tooltips stuffed with paragraphs disappear before they are read.
components.solution: Write the screen first: clear headings, labels and short descriptions. For anything that needs more, put an Info link next to the heading or label that opens the help panel on the right with page, section or field help. Each help topic ends with links to the full article.

steps.t: Small: headings, labels, one or two lines of description, and constraint text under fields. Most questions end here.
Medium: an Info link beside a page heading, section heading or field label opens the help panel at that topic.
With no Info link pressed, the help panel shows help for the whole page.
Large: the panel's Learn more list links to help centre articles, which open in a new tab so the task is not lost.
Closing and reopening the panel on the same page shows the last topic read, not the page default.

whenToUse.t: Decisions with consequences people may not know, such as what Visa sponsorship does to who can apply, or what Closing date means for applications in progress.
Concepts specific to the product, such as how pipeline stages map to candidate emails.
Every step of a multi-step create flow, such as Create listing.

whenNotToUse.t: To name an icon button or show its shortcut. Use a tooltip.
For questions about the records on screen, such as "which listings close this week". Use the assistant (⌘J).
On the home page or any page with nothing to explain. Never show an empty help panel.

guidelines.t: Place Info links next to headings and field labels only, never inside descriptions or body text.
The help topic's heading matches the heading or label it was opened from, word for word.
Help panel content is read-only reference. Forms and actions belong in the page or the side panel.
Requirements go in constraint text under the field before any error, not only in the help panel and never only in a placeholder.
Don't add standalone Learn more links on a page that has help panel content, except inside a banner or dialog.
Keep descriptions to one or two lines; longer explanation moves to the help panel.

content.t: Answer three questions in order: what is this, why does it matter, how do I choose.
Page headings start with a noun for views ("Listings") and a verb for tasks ("Create listing").
Info link text is "Info"; its accessible name adds the topic: "Info about Visa sponsorship".
Help centre links say where they go: "Learn how pipeline stages work", not "Click here".

accessibility.t: The help panel is a labelled complementary region; opening it from an Info link moves focus to the topic heading, and closing it returns focus to the link.
Info links are buttons (they open a panel), not links, and say which topic they open.
External help links are marked as opening in a new tab, in text and in the accessible name.

dos.t: Do write the label and description first; add help only for what they can't carry.
Do give every page that has decisions a page-level help topic.
Do open help centre articles in a new tab.

donts.t: Don't put paragraphs in tooltips.
Don't switch the panel back to the default topic when it is reopened.
Don't use the help panel as a form.

components.name: Secondary panels: which right-hand panel
components.summary: TwoUX has one right-hand panel slot. Record detail, the assistant, help and filters each have a clear job, only one is open at a time, and none is ever required to finish a task.
components.problem: When every feature adds its own panel, people can't tell which icon opens what, panels pile up and crush the table, and tasks end up depending on something hidden behind a toggle.
components.solution: Choose the panel by what the person is trying to do: look at a record (side panel), ask about the data (assistant panel), learn how something works (help panel), narrow a large search (filter panel). Opening one replaces the one already in the slot.

steps.t: Name the person's goal: review a record, get an answer about the data, learn the product, or narrow results.
Pick the panel: side panel for a record, assistant panel for questions, help panel for guidance, filter panel for searches with many fields.
Check the main task can be finished without the panel. If it can't, the content belongs in the page.
Open the panel only from a person's action; opening it moves the previous panel out of the slot, and closing it brings that panel back.

whenToUse.t: For supporting information or tools that relate to the page the person is on.
When the person benefits from seeing the list and the extra content side by side.
When the extra content should stay open while people move through records with J and K.

whenNotToUse.t: For a decision that must interrupt the task. Use a confirmation dialog.
For a long, standalone task such as editing a whole listing. Use a full page.
For content unrelated to the current page, such as account settings.

guidelines.t: At most three panel types on any page. If a fourth is needed, one of them is probably a page or a dialog.
Triggers sit in a fixed order wherever they appear: record detail opens from the row, then Assistant (⌘J), then Help.
Panels are secondary: they can speed a task up, but every task can be completed without opening one.
Help panel content is read-only; side panel, assistant and filter panel content can be interactive.
Below 860px the open panel takes the full width of the canvas and has a clear close button.

content.t: Trigger buttons have text or a tooltip with the panel name and shortcut: "Assistant ⌘J", "Help".
The panel heading names what is inside: the record title, "Assistant", or the help topic.
Close buttons are named for the panel: "Close help", "Close assistant".

accessibility.t: Every panel is a labelled complementary region, not a modal, unless it overlays content (then it follows the dialog pattern).
Opening a panel from a control moves focus into it; Esc closes it and focus returns to the control.
The panel never hides the focused element on the page (2.4.11).

dos.t: Do choose the panel from the person's goal.
Do keep panel triggers in the same order on every page.
Do restore the previous panel when the newer one closes.

donts.t: Don't open two right-hand panels at once.
Don't open a panel on page load.
Don't hide a required step inside a panel.

components.name: Collecting product feedback
components.summary: Ask "Was this helpful?" in a quiet spot after people have read or used something, record the Yes or No straight away, then offer one short optional question.
components.problem: Feedback pop-ups mid-task annoy people and get dismissed, long surveys get abandoned, and a free-text box in a hiring tool invites people to paste candidate names and other personal data.
components.solution: Use the feedback prompt at the end of help topics, reports and new features. A Yes or No vote is sent on its own. An optional follow-up of one to three questions appears after the vote, with a reminder not to include personal data.

steps.t: Place the prompt at the end of the content, after people have read or used it: the foot of a help topic, the end of a report, the side of a new feature's page.
Ask one specific question about that content: "Was this helpful?" with Yes and No.
Send the vote as soon as it is chosen. Show a loading state on the button, then a short thank you with the chosen answer.
After the vote, reveal an optional follow-up: one to three fields, such as "What was missing?". Send it separately.
If sending fails, say so beside the prompt and offer Try again.

whenToUse.t: At the end of each help topic and help centre article.
On a feature in beta, such as a new pipeline report, to learn whether it is useful.
After a new workflow is used for the first time, such as the first bulk extend, as a quiet line in the result banner rather than a pop-up.

whenNotToUse.t: On assistant answers. They have their own good and bad controls next to the origin label.
In a dialog or pop-up that interrupts a task.
For more than three questions. Link to a separate survey page instead.

guidelines.t: Never interrupt. The prompt sits in the page flow, never as a modal or a toast.
One prompt per page, with at most one follow-up form.
Keep the follow-up to three questions or fewer; more lowers response and adds data to process.
Free text carries a privacy line, and the feedback store strips email addresses and phone numbers before saving.
In a side panel, place the expanding follow-up so the page doesn't jump; on narrow screens, the prompt moves to the end of the content.
Don't promise a reply. Only say "We'll get back to you" if someone really will.

content.t: Question: "Was this helpful?" or "Was this report useful?". Answers: "Yes" and "No".
Thank you: "Thanks, your feedback is recorded." with the chosen answer shown as selected.
Privacy line under free text: "Don't include candidate names or other personal details."

accessibility.t: Yes and No are buttons with visible text, not icon-only thumbs.
After a successful vote, focus moves to the thank you message so it isn't lost.
Send errors are announced through a live region.

dos.t: Do record the vote before asking anything else.
Do ask about the specific content, not "How are we doing?".
Do keep the prompt in the page flow, at the end of the content.

donts.t: Don't show a feedback pop-up during a task.
Don't put two follow-up forms on one page.
Don't collect personal data in feedback free text.

components.name: Unsaved changes
components.summary: Don't let people lose work by accident: save drafts of long text automatically, and ask before discarding a changed form only when there really are changes.
components.problem: Someone writing a job description clicks a breadcrumb or closes the tab and loses twenty minutes of work. The opposite failure is a "Discard changes?" dialog that appears when nothing changed, which trains people to click through it.
components.solution: Track whether a form is dirty. Long text (job descriptions, email templates) saves a draft as people type. A changed form that would be lost by leaving asks once, in TwoUX's confirmation dialog, with Keep editing as the safe default. Browser-level exits use the browser's own prompt.

steps.t: Track a dirty flag per form: true once a value differs from what was loaded, false again after save or if the person changes it back.
For long text, save a draft every few seconds after typing stops and show "Draft saved 10 seconds ago" near the actions. A form whose draft is saved is not at risk, so no prompt is needed.
When an in-app action would throw unsaved changes away (Cancel, a breadcrumb, a side navigation link, J or K to the next record, Esc on a panel form), open the confirmation dialog.
While the form is dirty, register a beforeunload handler so closing or reloading the tab shows the browser's own prompt; remove it as soon as the form is clean.
After the person chooses Discard, carry out the action they started; after Keep editing, return focus to where they were.

whenToUse.t: Create listing, Edit listing and other multi-field forms with a Save button.
Forms inside the side panel, where J, K or Esc would move away from the edit.
Long text such as a job description or an email template, where autosaved drafts replace the prompt.

whenNotToUse.t: Inline edits in the data grid or side panel fields, which save on Enter or blur; there is never an unsaved state to lose.
When nothing has changed, everything is already saved, or the action opens a new tab.
When opening or closing a disclosure inside the same form, such as a Show advanced options section.

guidelines.t: Ask every time there is a risk of loss, whatever the size of the change; consistency means people never have to guess.
Never offer "Don't ask again" on this dialog; there would be no way to turn it back on.
Discarding typed work cannot be undone, so this is one of the few places TwoUX confirms instead of offering Undo.
Mark a dirty form in text near the Save button ("Unsaved changes"), not only with a dot.
If a save fails, keep the form dirty and its values in place, with the error in a banner above the actions.

content.t: Dialog title: "Discard changes to this listing?" Body: "Your changes to Junior Product Designer haven't been saved."
Buttons: "Keep editing" (safe, focused) and "Discard changes" (destructive). Not Yes and No.
Draft status: "Draft saved 10 seconds ago", or "Saving draft" while it saves.

accessibility.t: The dialog follows the alert dialog pattern: focus moves to Keep editing, Tab is trapped, Esc means Keep editing.
Draft saved status updates in a polite live region, at most once per save, so screen readers aren't flooded.
The browser's own beforeunload prompt is accessible by default; don't try to replace it with custom text.

dos.t: Do save drafts of long text automatically.
Do ask only when the form is dirty.
Do make Keep editing the default.

donts.t: Don't keep the beforeunload handler on a clean form.
Don't ask when someone opens a section inside the same form.
Don't add "Don't ask again".

components.name: Timestamps
components.summary: Show when things happened as relative time in lists ("3 hours ago"), the exact date and time on hover and in record details, and always say what the time refers to and who caused it.
components.problem: "12/03" means different days to different readers, times without a zone mislead remote teams, and a bare date in a column says nothing about whether it is when the listing was posted, edited or closes.
components.solution: Use the timestamp component everywhere. It renders relative time for past events in lists, absolute time in UK format in details and tooltips, and ISO 8601 in exports and code. Every timestamp has a label of noun and verb, and the person or system that made the change when it matters.

steps.t: Choose the format by the reader's need: how long ago (relative), exactly when (absolute), or a machine (ISO 8601).
Label it with what happened: "Posted", "Last edited", "Applied". In a table the label is the column header.
Add the source when it matters: "Edited 6 hours ago by Priya Shah", linked to their profile.
Give every relative time its absolute value on hover and focus, and in the accessible name.

whenToUse.t: Relative: activity feeds, Applied and Last edited columns, the Inbox, "Last updated" after a refresh.
Absolute: the Details section of a record, audit history, and deadlines such as a listing's closing date.
ISO 8601: CSV exports, API responses and anything people paste into code.

whenNotToUse.t: Relative time for deadlines. "Closes in 2 weeks" hides the actual day; show "Closes 20 November 2026", with "in 14 days" in muted text if useful.
Relative time for billing or usage periods; use the unit being counted, such as hours.
Durations such as time to hire. Show a number and unit ("18 days"), not a timestamp.

guidelines.t: Relative units: "Just now" under a minute, then minutes, hours, days, weeks, months and years ago, in the largest whole unit.
Absolute format in the UK: "6 November 2026, 14:32 GMT" (BST in summer). Teammates in other time zones see their own zone, and the zone is always shown.
Spell months and units in full in details and tooltips: "November", "minutes". Omit the year in tables when it is the current year.
Relative times refresh about once a minute without announcing each change.
When the change came from an applied assistant proposal, the source is the person, with "via Assistant": "Edited 2 minutes ago by Priya Shah via Assistant".

content.t: Labels are noun and verb, with no "date" or "time": "Listing posted", not "Posted date".
Past tense for things that happened ("Closed"), present or future for things to come ("Closes").
Add "Last" only for events that repeat: "Last edited", "Last updated".
In tables where rows start and end at different times, "[noun] [verb] time" is allowed: "Interview start time".

accessibility.t: Render with <time datetime="2026-11-06T14:32:00Z"> using the ISO value, and the absolute human date in the tooltip and accessible description.
Don't rely on the title attribute for the absolute time; it is not available to keyboard or touch users. Use TwoUX's tooltip on focus and hover.
Relative times that update do not sit inside a live region.

dos.t: Do label every timestamp with its event.
Do show the time zone on every absolute time.
Do use ISO 8601 in exports.

donts.t: Don't write numeric dates such as 06/11/2026; they read differently in the UK and US.
Don't abbreviate units: "5 minutes ago", not "5m ago", outside dense tables.
Don't show a relative deadline without the date.

components.name: Page actions and row actions
components.summary: Actions that affect the page or many records sit in the page header or the bulk action bar; one or two frequent actions also sit on each row, and every row action is reachable from the selection too.
components.problem: If row actions and page actions live in different places on every screen, people miss them. Rows crowded with buttons are noisy, and actions that exist only on hover can't be found by keyboard or touch users.
components.solution: Global actions (Create listing, Export, actions on a selection) live in the page header and the bulk action bar. In-context actions live with the thing they change: a row's last column, a card or section header. The full set is always available globally; in-context copies are shortcuts for the common ones.

steps.t: List every action and who it acts on: the page or collection (Create listing, Export), a selection (Close, Extend), or one record (Edit, Duplicate).
Put page actions in the page header: up to four buttons, with the single primary action last on the right; more go in a More actions menu.
Put selection actions in the bulk action bar. Any action that can apply to many records is offered there, so nobody repeats it row by row.
On rows, keep one or two of the most used actions as icon buttons and the rest in a More actions menu in the last column. Choose them from usage data.
Put actions for a section or card in that section's header, on the right.

whenToUse.t: Global: creating a record, exporting, importing, and any action on selected rows.
In-context: frequent one-record actions such as Duplicate listing or Copy link, and section actions such as Edit details in the side panel.
Section actions: Edit details on a side panel section, Add interviewer on an interview card.

whenNotToUse.t: Row menus for bulk actions. Bulk work belongs in the bulk action bar.
A primary button inside a row. Rows use icon buttons or a menu, never filled buttons.
Hover-only actions with no menu fallback; touch and keyboard users would never find them.

guidelines.t: One primary action per view, in the page header.
Header order from left to right: status actions (Pause, Reopen), View, Edit, other actions, Delete, then the primary action.
Row menus hold up to seven items, most used first, with destructive items last after a separator.
The More actions button on each row is always visible; quick icon buttons may appear on row hover or focus, and always on touch screens.
Keep the actions column sticky on wide tables so actions stay in view while scrolling sideways.
When an action depends on status, such as Reopen on a Closed listing, show the Status column so people see why it is offered.
Every action is also in the command palette (⌘K) with its shortcut.

content.t: Button labels are a verb, plus a noun when the verb alone is unclear: "Create listing", "Export", "Close 2 listings".
Menu buttons name their set: "More actions", not "Options" or an unlabelled dots icon.
No end punctuation in button or menu labels.

accessibility.t: Icon-only row actions have an accessible name that includes the record: "Duplicate Junior Product Designer".
The More actions button follows the menu button pattern: Enter or Space opens, arrows move, Esc closes and returns focus.
Hover-revealed icons also appear when the row has keyboard focus.

dos.t: Do keep the full action set in the header, bulk bar and ⌘K.
Do limit rows to one or two visible actions.
Do put the primary action last on the right.

donts.t: Don't make hover the only way to find a row action.
Don't put two primary buttons on one page.
Don't put actions for the whole table in a row menu.

components.name: Choosing a selection control
components.summary: Pick the control from three questions: one choice or many, how many options, and does it apply at once or on Save.
components.problem: The same kind of choice ends up as a radio group on one form, a dropdown on another and a switch on a third, so people can't predict when a change takes effect.
components.solution: One choice from up to seven: radio. One choice from eight or more: select. Many from up to seven: checkboxes. Many from eight or more: multiselect. On or off with immediate effect: switch. On or off applied on Save: checkbox. Two to three view options: segmented control.

steps.t: One option or many? Many means checkboxes or a multiselect.
How many options? Up to seven show all of them (radio or checkboxes); eight or more use a Combobox (combobox), with multiple for several.
For on or off: does it take effect at once (switch) or when the form is saved (checkbox)?
If both the on and off states need explaining, use two radio options with descriptions instead.

whenToUse.t: Radio: Work pattern on a listing (On-site, Hybrid, Remote (UK)).
Select: Location from the list of offices; multiselect: Skills from a long list.
Switch: "Email me when a listing closes" in notification settings, saved at once. Checkbox: "Offer visa sponsorship" in the Create listing form.

whenNotToUse.t: Segmented control for a form value. It switches views or settings of what is shown, such as Daily or Weekly.
A switch inside a form with a Save button; people expect a switch to act at once.
Any selection control for a filter on a list page; filters use the filter pills.

guidelines.t: When a choice reveals sub-options, use a different control for the parent than for the children: a checkbox that reveals radio options, not checkboxes inside checkboxes.
Place revealed sub-options after the whole radio group, never between two radio options.
Use the same parent control for the same kind of reveal everywhere on a page.
Order options logically: by frequency, by the order of the hiring process, or alphabetically for long lists.
Give options short descriptions only when they help people choose; keep the sentence structure the same across options.

content.t: Switch labels describe the setting when on: "Email me when a listing closes".
Checkbox labels describe what ticking does: "Offer visa sponsorship".
When every option shares a subject, put it in the group label ("Work pattern") and keep options short.

accessibility.t: Radio and checkbox groups are fieldsets with a legend that is the group label.
A switch uses role="switch" and announces on or off.
Revealed sub-options follow their parent in the focus order.

dos.t: Do show all options when there are seven or fewer.
Do use a switch only for changes that apply at once.
Do use radio options with descriptions when both on and off need explaining.

donts.t: Don't hide three options in a dropdown.
Don't nest the same control type for parent and sub-options.
Don't put controls between radio options.

components.name: Creating a record: dialog, single page or steps
components.summary: Pick the creation surface by how much people must decide: a small dialog for a name or two, one page for most records, steps only for long or high-stakes set-ups. Fill everything else with visible defaults.
components.problem: Each team builds creation differently: a wizard for a three-field listing, a modal stacked on a modal for a new location, forms that ask for things the product could have guessed. People abandon long forms and get lost in short wizards.
components.solution: Count the decisions people must make, not the fields that exist. Ask only for what has no good default; put the rest under Additional settings with the default showing. Use a dialog for up to three short fields, one page for most records, and the Stepper only when steps depend on each other, settings can't be changed after creation, or the result reaches people outside the workspace.

steps.t: List every field, then sort it: required with no good default, expected by at least 8 in 10 people (such as salary on a listing), and everything else. Only the first two groups go in the main section.

Choose the surface. A dialog for one to three short fields, such as a new saved view or a new tag. A single page for most records, such as Create listing. The Stepper for long or dependent set-ups, such as Publish listing to job boards. When fields appear based on earlier answers, count the longest version of the form.
Show defaults as real values in the fields: Closing date 6 December 2026 (30 days), Hiring manager: you. Values TwoUX decides later say so in the hint: "Reference number is assigned when you save."
Put the remaining fields in a collapsed Additional settings section at the end, each with its default filled in.
The primary button stays enabled. On submit, validate, show the error summary and move focus to the first problem.
On success, open the new record (side panel or page, as Record detail says) and show a toast such as "Listing created".

whenToUse.t: Dialog: one to three short fields that can all be changed later, with nothing to look up elsewhere.
Single page: most records, from a draft listing to a new candidate with CV upload, up to about 15 main fields or 5 groups.

Stepper: more than about 15 main fields or 5 groups, later steps that change with earlier answers, settings that cannot be changed after creation, or one group complex enough to need its own page, such as application questions with their own rules.
If length, complexity and recovery still leave it open, use frequency: one page for records people create often, steps for set-ups done rarely.

whenNotToUse.t: Don't use steps to make a short form feel lighter. Three steps of two fields each is slower than one page.
Don't use this for changing one value on an existing record. Use inline editing.
Don't create records the assistant suggested without the person applying the proposal. Use Propose, then apply.

guidelines.t: Order the main fields the way the list shows them. The field order on Create listing becomes the default column order in the Listings table.
Defaults must match what TwoUX will actually save. If the hint says "Closes after 30 days", the listing closes after 30 days.
Never ask for something the workspace already knows. Prefill the team, office address and hiring manager from the person and workspace.

When a field needs something that does not exist yet, such as a new location, offer "Create Leeds office" inside the select for a name only, or open an overlay side panel for more. When it is saved, select it in the field and return focus there.
Never stack a dialog on a dialog, and never run a Stepper inside a side panel or dialog.
Leaving with unsaved input asks "Discard new listing?" with Keep editing focused. Leaving an untouched form closes without asking.
Stepper flows: three to five steps, seven at most, one page per step, a Review step at the end with Edit links back to each step, in the same order as the steps.
In a Stepper, check each step when people press Next and keep them on it until it passes. The Review step checks everything again and links each problem to the step that holds it.

content.t: Page title and button use the same verb and object: page "Create listing", button "Create listing". Cancel is "Cancel".
Section headings are nouns: "Role", "Location and pay", "Additional settings". Not "Enter role details".
Hints say what happens if the field is left as it is: "If you leave this blank, the listing stays open until you close it."
Mark optional fields "(optional)"; don't mark required ones.

accessibility.t: One h1 per page (the page title); each section is an h2 in a labelled group.
Additional settings is a disclosure button with aria-expanded. When it opens, focus stays on the button.
The Stepper names the current step in text ("Step 2 of 4: Application questions") and moves focus to the step heading on Next and Back.
When a sub-create side panel closes, focus returns to the field that opened it.

dos.t: Do let people create with one press of Create when the defaults are right.
Do show every default in the field or hint, never hidden behind a setting.
Do keep the Review step free of editing; it links back to steps instead.

donts.t: Don't disable Create until the form is valid. Validate on submit and say what is missing.
Don't add a sidebar item for a create page; it opens from the page header of the list.
Don't open a dialog to create something from inside another dialog.

components.name: Editing a record: inline, section or whole page
components.summary: Change one value where it is shown, one section in place, or many linked settings on an edit page that mirrors the create form. Every saved edit can be undone.
components.problem: Some screens open a full form to change a closing date; others edit linked settings one cell at a time and leave the record half changed. Edit forms drift away from the create form, so people meet the same field in two shapes.
components.solution: Edit one value inline. Edit one section in place: it turns into a form with Save and Cancel. Use an edit page only when several settings depend on each other, and build it from the create form with the same fields in the same order. Saving shows a toast with Undo.

steps.t: Ask what is changing. One value on one or many records: inline. Several values in one section of a record: section edit. Settings that depend on each other across sections: edit page.
Inline: follow Inline editing and validation. Enter edits, Enter saves, Esc cancels.
Section edit: an Edit button in the section header turns that section into a form with Save and Cancel at its end. Other sections stay read-only.
Edit page: title "Edit Junior Product Designer", breadcrumb ending in "Edit", the create form's fields and sections in the same order, Save changes and Cancel at the end.
On save, return to where the edit started and show "Listing updated. Undo". With no changes, return and show "No changes made".

whenToUse.t: Inline: values people change often or across many rows, such as stage, owner or closing date.
Section edit: a group that belongs together, such as Location and pay on a listing.
Edit page: changes where one setting limits another, such as switching a listing from Internal to Public, which adds job board and salary rules.

whenNotToUse.t: Don't open an edit page to change one value.
Don't mix create and edit in one view, such as adding a new listing from inside the edit page of another.
Don't use edit for actions with their own consequence, such as Close listing or Reject candidate. They are actions with their own button and, where needed, confirmation.

guidelines.t: The edit page reuses the create form component, so labels, order, hints and validation never drift apart.
Save changes stays enabled. Validate on submit, keep the person's input, and show server errors above the buttons so nothing has to be typed again.
An edited row that no longer matches the filters or sort stays in place, marked, until the list refreshes, so it doesn't vanish under the cursor.
Lists of repeated values, such as screening questions or interview stages, use rows with Add and Remove. Removing a row takes effect on save and says so: "Removed when you save".
Leaving an edit with unsaved changes asks "Discard changes?" with Keep editing focused.
Every saved edit is reversible with Undo in the toast, ⌘Z and the record's activity.

content.t: Edit page title: "Edit" plus the record name. Submit button: "Save changes".
Section headings match the create form word for word.
Limits on repeated rows say what is left: "You can add 3 more questions."

accessibility.t: When a section switches to edit, focus moves to its first field; on Save or Cancel it returns to the section's Edit button.
Each Edit button names its section: aria-label "Edit location and pay".
When a repeated row is added, focus moves to its first input; when removed, focus moves to the next row or the Add button.

dos.t: Do edit in place when the change is small.
Do mirror the create form exactly on the edit page.
Do offer Undo after every saved edit.

donts.t: Don't disable Save changes until something changes.
Don't put two Edit modes on the screen at once; one section edits at a time.
Don't open a dialog to edit a section of a record that is already in a side panel.

components.name: Deleting records
components.summary: Deleting moves records to Deleted with Undo. Only permanent or cascading deletes ask first, and only the rare, severe ones ask people to type the name.
components.problem: Delete is where TwoUX's Undo-first rule meets real loss. Without a shared ladder, teams either confirm every removal or let a single click erase a candidate's history, and typed confirmations spread to places where they only slow people down.
components.solution: Four levels, chosen by what is lost and who it affects. Remove a part of a form you are editing at once. Delete a record to Deleted, with Undo. Permanently delete in a confirmation dialog that names what goes and what stays. Ask for the typed name only when the delete is permanent and takes other records with it.

steps.t: Remove a part of a form being edited, such as a screening question or a tag: no confirmation, it goes at once, with Undo where it saves straight away.
Delete a record, such as a draft listing or a duplicate candidate: it moves to Deleted, where it can be restored for 30 days. Show "Listing deleted. Undo".
Permanently delete, such as emptying Deleted or erasing a candidate on request: a confirmation dialog titled with the action and count, naming what goes and what stays.
Permanent and cascading, such as deleting a workspace or a team with live listings: the same dialog, plus a warning banner listing what else goes, and a field where the person types the name.

If something must happen first, such as closing a live listing that still has applicants, the dialog says so and links to it. The confirm field and button wait until it is done, and the reason is written in the dialog.

whenToUse.t: Deleted with Undo: the default for every record people can delete.
Confirmation dialog: anything that cannot come back, including bulk permanent deletes.
Typed name: permanent deletes that also remove other records or affect other people's work.

whenNotToUse.t: Don't use delete for ending a process. Closing a listing or rejecting a candidate are their own actions with their own wording.
Don't ask for a typed name on routine deletes. It slows people down and they learn to type without reading.
Don't let the assistant delete. It can propose a delete, which the person applies.

guidelines.t: Choose the level by three questions: can it come back, does it take other records with it, and what would it cost to redo.
The dialog body names the record in bold and states the result: "Permanently delete Priya Shah? Her application, notes and interview feedback are erased. You can't undo this."
Say what stays as well as what goes: "Reports keep the anonymised counts."
Typed confirmation: single record, type its name; bulk, type "delete". Matching ignores case and extra spaces, and paste works.
Always confirm in a dialog, never a popover or a separate page.
A bulk delete from the bulk action bar uses the level of its most severe item, and the title carries the count: "Permanently delete 12 candidates?"

content.t: Use "Remove" for taking something out of a form or list it still exists elsewhere in, and "Delete" for the record itself.
Dialog title is the action and count as a question: "Delete workspace?", "Permanently delete 3 listings?"
Buttons name the outcome: "Keep candidate" and "Delete permanently". Never "OK" or "Yes".
Typed confirmation label: "Type Leeds hiring team to confirm".

accessibility.t: Delete dialogs use role alertdialog with the title as the label and the consequence as the description.
Focus starts on the safe button, or on the typed confirmation field when there is one.
The typed confirmation field has a visible label naming the exact text, not only a placeholder.
After a delete, focus moves to the next row in the list, or the list heading if none is left, and the toast is announced.

dos.t: Do make Deleted the default and offer Undo.
Do state prerequisites in the dialog and link to them.
Do scale friction to severity and nothing more.

donts.t: Don't write "Are you sure?".
Don't focus the delete button by default.
Don't delete a live listing that has applicants in one step; ask people to close it first.

components.name: Navigation: what goes in the sidebar and the top bar
components.summary: The sidebar holds where you can go and the few things you always need; the top bar holds where you are and what this page does. Records never become sidebar items.
components.problem: Without a rule, global links land in page headers, record pages add themselves to the sidebar, and every feature adds a top-level item. People lose track of where they are and the sidebar turns into a site map.
components.solution: One app shell. The sidebar has three parts: the workspace menu with Search (⌘K) and Inbox at the top, the main sections in the middle, and Settings and Help at the bottom. The top bar shows the breadcrumb and page-level controls only. One sidebar item is always active, including on record pages.

steps.t: Top of the sidebar: the workspace menu (switch workspace, your profile, Preferences, Sign out last), then Search (⌘K) and Inbox with its count.
Middle: the main sections, ordered by how often a hiring team uses them: Home, Listings, Candidates, Interviews, Reports. Saved views sit under their section.
Bottom: Settings and Help, set apart by space or a divider.
Top bar: breadcrumb on the left, page-level controls such as the side panel toggle on the right. No global destinations.
On a record page, the record's type stays active in the sidebar: viewing Priya Shah keeps Candidates active.

whenToUse.t: For every screen inside the product.
When adding a new area: add a sidebar item only if people go there on its own, not only through a record.
When placing account and workspace utilities such as profile, preferences, Search and Inbox.

whenNotToUse.t: Not for sign-in, public careers pages or marketing pages. They have their own simple frame.
Don't use the sidebar for actions. Create listing lives in the Listings page header, not the sidebar.
Not for moving between records in a list. Use J and K with the side panel, as Record detail describes.

guidelines.t: Organise by the team's tasks and the things they manage, not by a site map. Create, edit and settings pages for one record are reached from the record, never from the sidebar.
Two levels at most. Deeper pages are reached through links in the page, and the breadcrumb shows the way back.
Group only when it helps: no group with only two links, and don't mix headed groups with expandable items in one sidebar.
Sidebar labels, breadcrumb items and page titles use the same words.
Counts in the sidebar are for things that need action, like Inbox. Saved views may show their live row count. No decorative counts or static labels other than New or Beta.
The sidebar is either shown in full or hidden; TwoUX has no icon-only rail. When hidden, Inbox keeps a small button with its count in the top bar.
Every destination is also reachable from ⌘K, so the sidebar is never the only way.

content.t: Section names are plural nouns for what they hold: "Listings", "Candidates". Not verbs or team jargon.
The workspace menu shows the workspace name and the person's name, so people with two workspaces know which one is open.
Breadcrumb items match sidebar labels: "Listings / Junior Product Designer".

accessibility.t: The sidebar is a nav landmark named "Main"; the breadcrumb is a nav named "Breadcrumb".
The active item has aria-current="page"; its look does not rely on colour alone.
A skip link to the main content is the first focusable item on every page.
The order of sidebar items is the same on every page.

dos.t: Do keep one sidebar item active on every page.
Do order items from most to least used.
Do put profile, preferences and sign out in the workspace menu, with Sign out last.

donts.t: Don't add a sidebar item when a record opens.
Don't put global links in the top bar or page header.
Don't add a top-level section for a feature people only reach from inside another one.

components.name: Announcing new and beta features
components.summary: Mark new or beta things where people meet them, with a small text label that opens a short explanation. Keep a What's new list for the rest. Never use toasts or banners for announcements.
components.problem: Launch messages compete with the messages people need to act on. Banners about a new report push down the list, popovers open on page load, and New labels stay for months until nobody notices them.
components.solution: A New or Beta text label sits next to the new thing for 30 days. Pressing it opens a popover of one or two sentences and Learn more. A What's new list in the Help menu keeps the last 90 days. Beta pages also carry "Beta" after the page title and a feedback link. Status messages always come first.

steps.t: Decide the size of the change. A new page or area: label in the sidebar. A new tab, column, field or option: label next to its name. A small fix: no label, What's new only.
Add a text label "New" (or "Beta") after the name. It is a button that opens a popover: a heading, one or two sentences on what it does for the team, and Learn more.
Remove New labels after 30 days. Beta labels stay until the feature is generally available.
Add the item to What's new in the Help menu, which shows an unread dot until opened.
For a beta page, add "Beta" after the page title too, since people arrive by links, with a line on what may change and a Send feedback link.

whenToUse.t: New: a whole new page, tab, column, field or option that changes what people can do.
Beta: a feature that may change, may be removed, or is not yet suitable for decisions that matter, such as an early AI shortlist summary.
A banner on Home only when the whole product or workspace is in beta. It cannot be dismissed on Home and can be elsewhere.

whenNotToUse.t: Not for bug fixes, speed improvements or small layout changes.
Never as a toast, an auto-opening popover or a page banner for a single feature. Those slots are for status.
Don't mark something both New and Beta. Beta wins.

guidelines.t: Status messages always win. If a page has an error or a warning, no announcement appears beside it.
The label is plain text in the accent colour at the caption size, not a status badge or a tag, so it is never mistaken for a record's state or a category.
Label each new page, never a group heading, so the label never competes with the group's own toggle.
Explanations lead with what the person can now do: "Compare time to hire across teams." Not the feature's name or the release.
Beta explanations say what that means for the work: "Results may change. Check them before you use them in a hiring decision."
Plan the end: a beta popover says when general availability is expected, if known.

content.t: Labels are one word: "New" or "Beta". TwoUX has no "Preview" state.
Popover heading names the capability: "Interview load by person". Not "Introducing...".
Beta page title: "Pipeline forecast" followed by the Beta label, not "Pipeline forecast (Beta version)".

accessibility.t: The label is a button with an accessible name such as "New: Interview load, more information", and opens its popover on Enter or Space.
The popover closes on Esc and returns focus to the label; it never opens on hover or page load.
The label is text, readable at the caption size against the sidebar background.

dos.t: Do announce in the place where the feature is used.
Do keep each explanation to two sentences and a link.
Do give every beta a way to send feedback.

donts.t: Don't open an announcement on page load.
Don't leave New labels beyond 30 days.
Don't rely on email or release notes alone to tell people a feature is in beta.
